Indeed, he was stubborn toward Our signs.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16] ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep climb.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17] ﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 18] ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19] ﴿Then may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 20] ﴿Then he looked.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 21] ﴿Then he frowned and scowled.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 22] ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 23] ﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic, transmitted.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 24] ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 25] ﴿I will burn him in Saqar.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26] ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 27] ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 28] ﴿It scorches the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 29] ﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30] ﴿We made the keepers of the Fire none but angels, and We made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain, and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did God intend by this as an example?"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]

**[p. 370]** This surah is Meccan; Ibn 'Atiyya said it is Meccan by consensus. In *al-Tahrir*, Muqatil said: except one verse, which is: ﴿We made their number only a trial﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

Its connection to what precedes it is that the preceding surah contains (*Leave me with the deniers*), and in it is ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]. So it fits with ﴿O you wrapped in your garment! Arise and warn!﴾. Then it mentions the Day of Judgment, and in His words ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11] it mentions some of the deniers.

The majority said: when he was frightened by seeing Gabriel on a chair between heaven and earth, and was terrified of him, he returned to Khadija and said: "Wrap me up, cover me." Then ﴿O you wrapped in your garment!﴾ was revealed. Al-Nakha'i, Qatada and 'A'isha said: he was called while he was in a state of wrapping himself, so he was addressed in one of his states. It is narrated that he had wrapped himself in a *qatifa* (a thick cloth). It was said: he used to hear from Quraysh what he disliked, so he grieved and covered himself with his garment in thought. So he was commanded not to abandon warning them, even if they made him hear and harmed him. 'Ikrima said its meaning: O you who are wrapped for prophethood and its burdens, as He said in *al-Muzzammil*.

Al-Jumhur read *al-muddaththir* with a shaddah on the *dal*. Its origin is *al-mutadaththir*, which was assimilated; it is likewise in the codex of Ubayy in its original form. 'Ikrima read it with a light *dal*, as *al-muzzammil* was read with a light *za'*, meaning: he wrapped himself. Also from 'Ikrima: the *ta'* is vowelled as a passive participle, and he said: "I have wrapped this matter, and it has been bound to you."

﴿Arise and warn!﴾ means: rise from your bed, or *qum* means to begin something, as you say: "Zayd stood up hitting 'Amr," meaning he began. As the poet said:

*Why did the base man begin insulting me?*

Meaning he began. The meaning is: rise with resolve and determination. ﴿And warn!﴾ means: warn of God's punishment and its events. Warning is general to all people, and it is his mission to creation.

﴿And magnify your Lord!﴾ means: glorify His greatness. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Your Lord is singled out for magnifying, which is describing Him with greatness and saying 'God is the Greatest.'" End of quote. This is according to his school, that placing the object before the verb indicates exclusivity. He said: the *fa'* enters for the sense of a condition, as if it were said: "Whatever is, do not neglect glorifying Him." End of quote. This is close to what the grammarians assumed in your saying: *Zaydan fa-idrib* ("Zayd, so strike him"). They said its assumption is: "Be alert, then strike Zayd." So the *fa'* is the answer to the imperative, and this imperative either contains the sense of a condition, or the condition after it is omitted, according to the disagreement among the grammarians about it.

﴿And purify your garments!﴾: The apparent meaning is that he was commanded to purify the garments from impurities, because the purity of garments is a condition for the validity of prayer, and it would be ugly for a believer's garments to be impure. The view that it is literally garments is the view of Ibn Sirin, Ibn Zayd and al-Shafi'i. From this verse al-Shafi'i held that washing impurity from the garment of one praying is obligatory. It was said: its purification is its shortening, and opposing the Arabs in lengthening garments and dragging their trains as a matter of pride and arrogance. The poet said:

*Then they went out, fragrant with musk, sweeping the earth with the fringes of their waist-wraps.*

One is not safe from their being struck by impurity. In a hadith: "The lower garment of the believer reaches to the middle of his shins; there is no blame on him between that and the ankles; what is below that is in the Fire." The majority held that "garments" here is metaphorical. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: its purification is that it not be soiled with filth. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr also said: garments are a metaphor for the heart, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*So take off my garments from your garments.*

Meaning: my heart from your heart. And it is about purity from filth, and he recited the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salama al-Thaqafi:

*Indeed, by the praise of God, I have not put on a treacherous garment, nor do I cover myself with disgrace.*

It was said: it is a metaphor for the purity of deeds, meaning: "And make your deeds righteous." Said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Zayd said: when a man's deeds are evil, they say: "So-and-so has evil garments," and when his deeds are good, they say: "So-and-so has pure garments." Similar to this is from al-Suddi. From this is the poet's saying:

*O God, indeed 'Amir ibn Jahm, or he blamed the pilgrimage in greasy garments.*

Meaning: he soiled it with sins. It was said: garments is a metaphor for the self, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The poet said:

*So I pierced with the long spear his garments.*

Another said:

*The garments of the Banu 'Awf are pure and clean, and their faces are white, clearly bright.*

Meaning: their selves. It was said: garments is a metaphor for the body. Layla said, mentioning camels:

*They threw them with light garments, and we see no likeness of them except the scattered ostriches.*

Meaning: they rode them and threw themselves onto them. It was said: it is a metaphor for the family. God said: ﴿They are garments for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], and purifying oneself with them is choosing chaste believing women. It was said: having intercourse with them in the front passage and not the back, in a state of purity and not during menstruation, related by Ibn Bahr. It was said: it is a metaphor for character, meaning: "And beautify your character." Said by al-Hasan and al-Qurtubi, and from this is his saying:

*Yahya who does not suit evil character, and Yahya the pure of garments, free.*

[p. 372]

That is: good in character. The majority of reciters read ﴿والرِّجْزَ﴾ (*al-rijza*) with a kasra on the rāʾ, which is the dialect of the Quraysh. Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Sulamī, Abū Jaʿfar, Abū Shayba, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ibn Wathhāb, Qatāda, al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-Aʿraj and Ḥafṣ read it with a ḍamma. Some said the two forms have the same meaning, both referring to idols and images. Others said that the kasra refers to separation, shortcomings and immorality, while the ḍamma refers to two idols, Asāf and Nāʾila. ʿIkrima, Mujāhid and al-Zuhrī said it refers to idols in general. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *al-rujz* is wrath, meaning: abandon what leads to it. al-Ḥasan said: it is every act of disobedience, and the meaning of the command is: persist and remain steadfast in abandoning it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was innocent of it. al-Nakhaʿī said: *al-rujz* is sin. al-Qutaybī said: it is punishment, meaning: abandon what leads to it.

The majority read ﴿ولا تَمْنُنْ﴾ (*wa lā tamnun*) with the doubled consonant separated (*fakk al-taḍʿīf*). al-Ḥasan and Abū al-Simmāl read it with the nūn doubled (*shadd al-nūn*). Ibn ʿAbbās and others said: do not give a gift in order to receive more than it. It seems to derive from their saying *manna* when someone gives. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: this is specific to him (ﷺ), and it is permitted for his community, but they will have no reward for it. Also from Ibn ʿAbbās: do not say, "I called, but I was not answered." From Qatāda: do not rely on your deeds. From Ibn Zayd: do not boast of your prophethood, seeking more reward or gain from them. al-Ḥasan said: do not confer favor upon God by your diligence, considering your deeds great and feeling self-admiration because of them. All these statements are forms of *manna*, which is counting and mentioning a favor. Mujāhid said: ﴿ولا تَمْنُنْ تَسْتَكْثِرُ﴾ means: [do not regard as great] what We have burdened you with of the weights of the message, or [do not seek to increase] good. This derives from their saying *ḥablun matīn*, meaning weak. It was also said: do not give to someone while regarding what you give as great and seeing it as much.

The majority read ﴿تَسْتَكْثِرُ﴾ (*tastakthiru*) with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, and the clause is circumstantial (*ḥāliyya*, a clause describing the state of the subject), meaning: seeking more. al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible with the ḍamma that *an* be elided from it and its governing effect be cancelled, as was narrated: *aḥḍuru al-wagha* with a ḍamma. End of his words. This cannot be used to interpret the Qur'an, because such a usage is permitted only in poetry, and we have a sound alternative in the circumstantial reading, meaning: seeking more.

al-Ḥasan and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with a jazm (*jazm*, the absence of final vowel) on the rāʾ. The explanation is that it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿تَمْنُنْ﴾, meaning: do not seek more. This is like His saying ﴿يُضاعَفْ لَهُ العَذابُ﴾ [al-Furqān: 69] in the reading of those who used the jazm, as a substitute for the phrase *yalqa*. And like the poet's saying:

*If you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firewood, thick and coarse, and a fire blazing.*

This would be from the *manna* mentioned in His saying: ﴿لا تُبْطِلُوا صَدَقاتِكم بِالمَنِّ والأذى﴾ [al-Baqara: 264], "Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury," because it is the nature of the one who confers favor to regard what he gives as much and to count it significant. al-Zamakhsharī permitted two possibilities in it: first, that *tastakthiru* be made like *taʿḍudu* and be pronounced with sukūn for lightness; second, that the pause form be considered, so that the connected form follows the pause form. Neither may be used to interpret the Qur'an when there is a stronger reading, namely the substitute.

al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash also read ﴿تَسْتَكْثِرَ﴾ with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, meaning: you will not belittle it. Ibn Masʿūd read ﴿أنْ تَسْتَكْثِرَ﴾ with the particle *an* made explicit.

﴿ولِرَبِّكَ فاصْبِرْ﴾ means: for the sake of your Lord, He commanded him to be patient. This covers patience with the burdens of prophethood, with carrying out obedience to God, and with the harm of the disbelievers. Ibn Zayd said: [be patient] in the face of war with the red and the black, so every matter one is patient in and every matter one is patient from falls within patience. al-Zamakhsharī said: the *fā'* in His saying ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ﴾ indicates causation, as if it were said: be patient with their harm, for before them is a difficult day in which they will meet the consequence of their harm, and you will meet the consequence of your patience with it.

al-Zamakhsharī also said: the *fā'* in (*fa-dhālika*) indicates the response (*jazāʾ*). (If you ask): with what is *idhā* (when) in the accusative? And how is it correct for *yawmiʾidhin* (on that day) to be the adverbial complement of ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾ (a difficult day)? (I answer): *idhā* is in the accusative by what the response clause indicates, because the meaning is: ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ في النّاقُورِ﴾ (when the trumpet is sounded), the matter becomes difficult for the disbelievers. As for the one who permitted *yawmiʾidhin* to be the adverbial complement of ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾, the meaning is: that time of the sounding is the occurrence of a difficult day, because the Day of Resurrection comes and occurs at the moment the trumpet is sounded. It is also permissible for *yawmiʾidhin* to be a built form (*mabnī*) in the nominative position as a substitute for *dhālika*, with ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾ as the predicate, as if it were said: so the Day of the sounding is a difficult day. (If you ask): what is the benefit of His saying ﴿غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ﴾ (not easy), when *ʿasīr* (difficult) would suffice without it? (I answer): when He said ﴿عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾ (upon the disbelievers), restricting the difficulty to them, He said ﴿غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ﴾ to indicate that it is not for them as it is for the believers, an easy and light matter. Thus it combines a threat to the disbelievers with an increase in their rage, and good news and consolation for the believers. It is also permissible that it means a difficulty not expected to become easy, as with the difficulty of worldly affairs that is hoped to become easy. End of his words.

al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿فَإذا﴾ *idhā* is connected to ﴿أنْذِرْ﴾ (warn), meaning: warn them when the trumpet is sounded. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: according to the view of al-Akhfash, *idhā* may be a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with *fa-dhālika* as its predicate and the *fā'* being extra. As for *yawmiʾidhin*, it is an adverbial complement of *dhālika*. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted *ʿalā al-kāfirīn* to be connected to *yasīr*, meaning: not easy upon the disbelievers. It should not be permitted, because it places the object of the governing word (what is attached to *ghayr*) before the governing word itself, which is prohibited according to the sound view, though some permitted it, saying: *anā bi-Zaydin ghayru rāḍin* (I am not content with Zayd).

**[p. 368]** Surah al-Muddaththir (Meccan), fifty-six verses.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿O you wrapped in your garment!﴾ ﴿Arise and warn!﴾ ﴿And magnify your Lord!﴾ ﴿And purify your garments!﴾ ﴿And shun the idol!﴾ ﴿And do not give seeking more.﴾ ﴿And for your Lord, be patient.﴾ ﴿For when the trumpet is sounded,﴾ ﴿that will be a difficult day,﴾ ﴿not easy for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11] ﴿and to whom I gave abundant wealth,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 12] ﴿and sons present with him,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 13] ﴿and whom I made comfortable in every way.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 14] ﴿Then he desires that I should increase him more.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 15] ﴿No! Indeed, he was stubborn toward Our signs.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16] ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep climb.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17] ﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 18] ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19] ﴿Then may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 20] ﴿Then he looked.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 21] ﴿Then he frowned and scowled.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 22] ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 23] ﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic, transmitted.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 24] ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 25] ﴿I will burn him in Saqar.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26] ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 27] ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 28] ﴿It scorches the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 29] ﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30] ﴿We made the keepers of the Fire none but angels, and We made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain, and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did God intend by this as an example?" Thus God leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him. And it is nothing but a reminder to the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31] ﴿No! By the moon,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 32] ﴿and by the night when it withdraws,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 33] ﴿and by the morning when it brightens,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 34] ﴿indeed, it is one of the greatest things,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 35] ﴿a warning to the human being,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 36] ﴿to whoever among you wishes to go forward or to lag behind.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 37] ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38] ﴿except the companions of the right,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 39] ﴿in gardens, they ask one another﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 40] ﴿about the criminals:﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 41] ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42] ﴿They will say, "We were not of those who prayed,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43] ﴿and we did not feed the needy,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 44] ﴿and we used to plunge with the plungers,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 45] ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 46] ﴿until the certainty came to us."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 47] ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48] ﴿What is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49] ﴿As if they were startled donkeys﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 50] ﴿fleeing from a lion.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 51] ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 52] ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 53] ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 54] ﴿so whoever wills may remember it.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 55] ﴿And they will not remember unless God wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 56]

*Tadaththara*: he put on the *didar* (dithar), which is the garment worn over the *shi'ar*. The *shi'ar* is the garment that lies next to the body. From this is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "The Ansar are the *shi'ar* (inner garment), and the people are the *didar* (outer garment)."

*Al-naqr*: the sound. The poet said:

*I lower it with the naqr when I have mounted it, and it raises a gaze that is not hidden, lowered.*

And the rajaz poet said:

*I am the son of Mawiyya, when the naqr became intense.*

He means *al-naqr*, and he transferred the vowel. So *al-naqur* is *fa'ul* from it, like *al-jasus* derived from *al-tajassus*.

*Abasa* (yaabisu, *abs*, *ubus*): he frowned. *Al-abs* is what clings to the tails of camels of their dung and urine. Abu al-Najm said:

*As if on their tails were the young camels, from the dung of the summer, the horns of the gazelles.*

*Basar*: he gathered what is between his eyes, and his face became pale. He said:

*We accompanied Tamim on the morning of al-Jifar, with a dark, blameworthy, scowling (bāsira) grey horse.*

The people of Yemen say: *basara al-markab* and *absara* when the ship stopped, and we have *absarna*. The Arabs say: "a scowling face, clearly scowling," when it changed and blackened.

*Lahahu al-basr*: it changed his form. He said:

*She says, "What has changed you, traveller? O daughter of my uncle, the heat has changed me."*

Another said:

*Hind wonders if she sees me pale, saying to something the hot winds have scorched.*

Al-Akhfash said: *al-luh* is the intensity of thirst. *Lahahu al-atash* and *lawwahahu* mean it changed him. The poet said:

*She gave me a drink of water on a pale, dry tongue, may God give it abundant, flowing rain.*

It is said: *iltah*, meaning he became thirsty.

*Al-qaswara*: the archers and hunters, said by Ibn Kaysan. Or the lion, said by a group of lexicographers. He said:

*A hidden one the heroes pursue, as if he were a lion, a fierce tiger.*

Or the strong men. Labid said:

*When we shout a shout in our assembly, the men who hunt come to us, the hunters.*

Or the darkness of the beginning of the night, not the darkness of its end, said by Ibn al-A'rabi and Tha'lab.

Indeed, he was stubborn toward Our signs.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16] ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep climb.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17] ﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 18] ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19] ﴿Then may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 20] ﴿Then he looked.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 21] ﴿Then he frowned and scowled.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 22] ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 23] ﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic, transmitted.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 24] ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 25] ﴿I will burn him in Saqar.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26] ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 27] ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 28] ﴿It scorches the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 29] ﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30] ﴿We made the keepers of the Fire none but angels, and We made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain, and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did God intend by this as an example?"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]

**[p. 370]** This surah is Meccan; Ibn 'Atiyya said it is Meccan by consensus. In *al-Tahrir*, Muqatil said: except one verse, which is: ﴿We made their number only a trial﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

Its connection to what precedes it is that the preceding surah contains (*Leave me with the deniers*), and in it is ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]. So it fits with ﴿O you wrapped in your garment! Arise and warn!﴾. Then it mentions the Day of Judgment, and in His words ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11] it mentions some of the deniers.

The majority said: when he was frightened by seeing Gabriel on a chair between heaven and earth, and was terrified of him, he returned to Khadija and said: "Wrap me up, cover me." Then ﴿O you wrapped in your garment!﴾ was revealed. Al-Nakha'i, Qatada and 'A'isha said: he was called while he was in a state of wrapping himself, so he was addressed in one of his states. It is narrated that he had wrapped himself in a *qatifa* (a thick cloth). It was said: he used to hear from Quraysh what he disliked, so he grieved and covered himself with his garment in thought. So he was commanded not to abandon warning them, even if they made him hear and harmed him. 'Ikrima said its meaning: O you who are wrapped for prophethood and its burdens, as He said in *al-Muzzammil*.

Al-Jumhur read *al-muddaththir* with a shaddah on the *dal*. Its origin is *al-mutadaththir*, which was assimilated; it is likewise in the codex of Ubayy in its original form. 'Ikrima read it with a light *dal*, as *al-muzzammil* was read with a light *za'*, meaning: he wrapped himself. Also from 'Ikrima: the *ta'* is vowelled as a passive participle, and he said: "I have wrapped this matter, and it has been bound to you."

﴿Arise and warn!﴾ means: rise from your bed, or *qum* means to begin something, as you say: "Zayd stood up hitting 'Amr," meaning he began. As the poet said:

*Why did the base man begin insulting me?*

Meaning he began. The meaning is: rise with resolve and determination. ﴿And warn!﴾ means: warn of God's punishment and its events. Warning is general to all people, and it is his mission to creation.

﴿And magnify your Lord!﴾ means: glorify His greatness. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Your Lord is singled out for magnifying, which is describing Him with greatness and saying 'God is the Greatest.'" End of quote. This is according to his school, that placing the object before the verb indicates exclusivity. He said: the *fa'* enters for the sense of a condition, as if it were said: "Whatever is, do not neglect glorifying Him." End of quote. This is close to what the grammarians assumed in your saying: *Zaydan fa-idrib* ("Zayd, so strike him"). They said its assumption is: "Be alert, then strike Zayd." So the *fa'* is the answer to the imperative, and this imperative either contains the sense of a condition, or the condition after it is omitted, according to the disagreement among the grammarians about it.

﴿And purify your garments!﴾: The apparent meaning is that he was commanded to purify the garments from impurities, because the purity of garments is a condition for the validity of prayer, and it would be ugly for a believer's garments to be impure. The view that it is literally garments is the view of Ibn Sirin, Ibn Zayd and al-Shafi'i. From this verse al-Shafi'i held that washing impurity from the garment of one praying is obligatory. It was said: its purification is its shortening, and opposing the Arabs in lengthening garments and dragging their trains as a matter of pride and arrogance. The poet said:

*Then they went out, fragrant with musk, sweeping the earth with the fringes of their waist-wraps.*

One is not safe from their being struck by impurity. In a hadith: "The lower garment of the believer reaches to the middle of his shins; there is no blame on him between that and the ankles; what is below that is in the Fire." The majority held that "garments" here is metaphorical. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: its purification is that it not be soiled with filth. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr also said: garments are a metaphor for the heart, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*So take off my garments from your garments.*

Meaning: my heart from your heart. And it is about purity from filth, and he recited the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salama al-Thaqafi:

*Indeed, by the praise of God, I have not put on a treacherous garment, nor do I cover myself with disgrace.*

It was said: it is a metaphor for the purity of deeds, meaning: "And make your deeds righteous." Said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Zayd said: when a man's deeds are evil, they say: "So-and-so has evil garments," and when his deeds are good, they say: "So-and-so has pure garments." Similar to this is from al-Suddi. From this is the poet's saying:

*O God, indeed 'Amir ibn Jahm, or he blamed the pilgrimage in greasy garments.*

Meaning: he soiled it with sins. It was said: garments is a metaphor for the self, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The poet said:

*So I pierced with the long spear his garments.*

Another said:

*The garments of the Banu 'Awf are pure and clean, and their faces are white, clearly bright.*

Meaning: their selves. It was said: garments is a metaphor for the body. Layla said, mentioning camels:

*They threw them with light garments, and we see no likeness of them except the scattered ostriches.*

Meaning: they rode them and threw themselves onto them. It was said: it is a metaphor for the family. God said: ﴿They are garments for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], and purifying oneself with them is choosing chaste believing women. It was said: having intercourse with them in the front passage and not the back, in a state of purity and not during menstruation, related by Ibn Bahr. It was said: it is a metaphor for character, meaning: "And beautify your character." Said by al-Hasan and al-Qurtubi, and from this is his saying:

*Yahya who does not suit evil character, and Yahya the pure of garments, free.*

[p. 372]

That is: good in character. The majority of reciters read ﴿والرِّجْزَ﴾ (*al-rijza*) with a kasra on the rāʾ, which is the dialect of the Quraysh. Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Sulamī, Abū Jaʿfar, Abū Shayba, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ibn Wathhāb, Qatāda, al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-Aʿraj and Ḥafṣ read it with a ḍamma. Some said the two forms have the same meaning, both referring to idols and images. Others said that the kasra refers to separation, shortcomings and immorality, while the ḍamma refers to two idols, Asāf and Nāʾila. ʿIkrima, Mujāhid and al-Zuhrī said it refers to idols in general. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *al-rujz* is wrath, meaning: abandon what leads to it. al-Ḥasan said: it is every act of disobedience, and the meaning of the command is: persist and remain steadfast in abandoning it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was innocent of it. al-Nakhaʿī said: *al-rujz* is sin. al-Qutaybī said: it is punishment, meaning: abandon what leads to it.

The majority read ﴿ولا تَمْنُنْ﴾ (*wa lā tamnun*) with the doubled consonant separated (*fakk al-taḍʿīf*). al-Ḥasan and Abū al-Simmāl read it with the nūn doubled (*shadd al-nūn*). Ibn ʿAbbās and others said: do not give a gift in order to receive more than it. It seems to derive from their saying *manna* when someone gives. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: this is specific to him (ﷺ), and it is permitted for his community, but they will have no reward for it. Also from Ibn ʿAbbās: do not say, "I called, but I was not answered." From Qatāda: do not rely on your deeds. From Ibn Zayd: do not boast of your prophethood, seeking more reward or gain from them. al-Ḥasan said: do not confer favor upon God by your diligence, considering your deeds great and feeling self-admiration because of them. All these statements are forms of *manna*, which is counting and mentioning a favor. Mujāhid said: ﴿ولا تَمْنُنْ تَسْتَكْثِرُ﴾ means: [do not regard as great] what We have burdened you with of the weights of the message, or [do not seek to increase] good. This derives from their saying *ḥablun matīn*, meaning weak. It was also said: do not give to someone while regarding what you give as great and seeing it as much.

The majority read ﴿تَسْتَكْثِرُ﴾ (*tastakthiru*) with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, and the clause is circumstantial (*ḥāliyya*, a clause describing the state of the subject), meaning: seeking more. al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible with the ḍamma that *an* be elided from it and its governing effect be cancelled, as was narrated: *aḥḍuru al-wagha* with a ḍamma. End of his words. This cannot be used to interpret the Qur'an, because such a usage is permitted only in poetry, and we have a sound alternative in the circumstantial reading, meaning: seeking more.

al-Ḥasan and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with a jazm (*jazm*, the absence of final vowel) on the rāʾ. The explanation is that it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿تَمْنُنْ﴾, meaning: do not seek more. This is like His saying ﴿يُضاعَفْ لَهُ العَذابُ﴾ [al-Furqān: 69] in the reading of those who used the jazm, as a substitute for the phrase *yalqa*. And like the poet's saying:

*If you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firewood, thick and coarse, and a fire blazing.*

This would be from the *manna* mentioned in His saying: ﴿لا تُبْطِلُوا صَدَقاتِكم بِالمَنِّ والأذى﴾ [al-Baqara: 264], "Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury," because it is the nature of the one who confers favor to regard what he gives as much and to count it significant. al-Zamakhsharī permitted two possibilities in it: first, that *tastakthiru* be made like *taʿḍudu* and be pronounced with sukūn for lightness; second, that the pause form be considered, so that the connected form follows the pause form. Neither may be used to interpret the Qur'an when there is a stronger reading, namely the substitute.

al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash also read ﴿تَسْتَكْثِرَ﴾ with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, meaning: you will not belittle it. Ibn Masʿūd read ﴿أنْ تَسْتَكْثِرَ﴾ with the particle *an* made explicit.

﴿ولِرَبِّكَ فاصْبِرْ﴾ means: for the sake of your Lord, He commanded him to be patient. This covers patience with the burdens of prophethood, with carrying out obedience to God, and with the harm of the disbelievers. Ibn Zayd said: [be patient] in the face of war with the red and the black, so every matter one is patient in and every matter one is patient from falls within patience. al-Zamakhsharī said: the *fā'* in His saying ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ﴾ indicates causation, as if it were said: be patient with their harm, for before them is a difficult day in which they will meet the consequence of their harm, and you will meet the consequence of your patience with it.

al-Zamakhsharī also said: the *fā'* in (*fa-dhālika*) indicates the response (*jazāʾ*). (If you ask): with what is *idhā* (when) in the accusative? And how is it correct for *yawmiʾidhin* (on that day) to be the adverbial complement of ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾ (a difficult day)? (I answer): *idhā* is in the accusative by what the response clause indicates, because the meaning is: ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ في النّاقُورِ﴾ (when the trumpet is sounded), the matter becomes difficult for the disbelievers. As for the one who permitted *yawmiʾidhin* to be the adverbial complement of ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾, the meaning is: that time of the sounding is the occurrence of a difficult day, because the Day of Resurrection comes and occurs at the moment the trumpet is sounded. It is also permissible for *yawmiʾidhin* to be a built form (*mabnī*) in the nominative position as a substitute for *dhālika*, with ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾ as the predicate, as if it were said: so the Day of the sounding is a difficult day. (If you ask): what is the benefit of His saying ﴿غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ﴾ (not easy), when *ʿasīr* (difficult) would suffice without it? (I answer): when He said ﴿عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾ (upon the disbelievers), restricting the difficulty to them, He said ﴿غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ﴾ to indicate that it is not for them as it is for the believers, an easy and light matter. Thus it combines a threat to the disbelievers with an increase in their rage, and good news and consolation for the believers. It is also permissible that it means a difficulty not expected to become easy, as with the difficulty of worldly affairs that is hoped to become easy. End of his words.

al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿فَإذا﴾ *idhā* is connected to ﴿أنْذِرْ﴾ (warn), meaning: warn them when the trumpet is sounded. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: according to the view of al-Akhfash, *idhā* may be a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with *fa-dhālika* as its predicate and the *fā'* being extra. As for *yawmiʾidhin*, it is an adverbial complement of *dhālika*. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted *ʿalā al-kāfirīn* to be connected to *yasīr*, meaning: not easy upon the disbelievers. It should not be permitted, because it places the object of the governing word (what is attached to *ghayr*) before the governing word itself, which is prohibited according to the sound view, though some permitted it, saying: *anā bi-Zaydin ghayru rāḍin* (I am not content with Zayd).

**[p. 368]** Surah al-Muddaththir (Meccan), fifty-six verses.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿O you wrapped in your garment!﴾ ﴿Arise and warn!﴾ ﴿And magnify your Lord!﴾ ﴿And purify your garments!﴾ ﴿And shun the idol!﴾ ﴿And do not give seeking more.﴾ ﴿And for your Lord, be patient.﴾ ﴿For when the trumpet is sounded,﴾ ﴿that will be a difficult day,﴾ ﴿not easy for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11] ﴿and to whom I gave abundant wealth,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 12] ﴿and sons present with him,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 13] ﴿and whom I made comfortable in every way.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 14] ﴿Then he desires that I should increase him more.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 15] ﴿No! Indeed, he was stubborn toward Our signs.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16] ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep climb.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17] ﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 18] ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19] ﴿Then may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 20] ﴿Then he looked.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 21] ﴿Then he frowned and scowled.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 22] ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 23] ﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic, transmitted.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 24] ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 25] ﴿I will burn him in Saqar.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26] ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 27] ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 28] ﴿It scorches the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 29] ﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30] ﴿We made the keepers of the Fire none but angels, and We made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain, and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did God intend by this as an example?" Thus God leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him. And it is nothing but a reminder to the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31] ﴿No! By the moon,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 32] ﴿and by the night when it withdraws,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 33] ﴿and by the morning when it brightens,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 34] ﴿indeed, it is one of the greatest things,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 35] ﴿a warning to the human being,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 36] ﴿to whoever among you wishes to go forward or to lag behind.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 37] ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38] ﴿except the companions of the right,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 39] ﴿in gardens, they ask one another﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 40] ﴿about the criminals:﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 41] ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42] ﴿They will say, "We were not of those who prayed,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43] ﴿and we did not feed the needy,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 44] ﴿and we used to plunge with the plungers,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 45] ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 46] ﴿until the certainty came to us."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 47] ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48] ﴿What is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49] ﴿As if they were startled donkeys﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 50] ﴿fleeing from a lion.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 51] ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 52] ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 53] ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 54] ﴿so whoever wills may remember it.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 55] ﴿And they will not remember unless God wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 56]

*Tadaththara*: he put on the *didar* (dithar), which is the garment worn over the *shi'ar*. The *shi'ar* is the garment that lies next to the body. From this is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "The Ansar are the *shi'ar* (inner garment), and the people are the *didar* (outer garment)."

*Al-naqr*: the sound. The poet said:

*I lower it with the naqr when I have mounted it, and it raises a gaze that is not hidden, lowered.*

And the rajaz poet said:

*I am the son of Mawiyya, when the naqr became intense.*

He means *al-naqr*, and he transferred the vowel. So *al-naqur* is *fa'ul* from it, like *al-jasus* derived from *al-tajassus*.

*Abasa* (yaabisu, *abs*, *ubus*): he frowned. *Al-abs* is what clings to the tails of camels of their dung and urine. Abu al-Najm said:

*As if on their tails were the young camels, from the dung of the summer, the horns of the gazelles.*

*Basar*: he gathered what is between his eyes, and his face became pale. He said:

*We accompanied Tamim on the morning of al-Jifar, with a dark, blameworthy, scowling (bāsira) grey horse.*

The people of Yemen say: *basara al-markab* and *absara* when the ship stopped, and we have *absarna*. The Arabs say: "a scowling face, clearly scowling," when it changed and blackened.

*Lahahu al-basr*: it changed his form. He said:

*She says, "What has changed you, traveller? O daughter of my uncle, the heat has changed me."*

Another said:

*Hind wonders if she sees me pale, saying to something the hot winds have scorched.*

Al-Akhfash said: *al-luh* is the intensity of thirst. *Lahahu al-atash* and *lawwahahu* mean it changed him. The poet said:

*She gave me a drink of water on a pale, dry tongue, may God give it abundant, flowing rain.*

It is said: *iltah*, meaning he became thirsty.

*Al-qaswara*: the archers and hunters, said by Ibn Kaysan. Or the lion, said by a group of lexicographers. He said:

*A hidden one the heroes pursue, as if he were a lion, a fierce tiger.*

Or the strong men. Labid said:

*When we shout a shout in our assembly, the men who hunt come to us, the hunters.*

Or the darkness of the beginning of the night, not the darkness of its end, said by Ibn al-A'rabi and Tha'lab.

Indeed, he was stubborn toward Our signs.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16] ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep climb.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17] ﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 18] ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19] ﴿Then may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 20] ﴿Then he looked.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 21] ﴿Then he frowned and scowled.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 22] ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 23] ﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic, transmitted.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 24] ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 25] ﴿I will burn him in Saqar.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26] ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 27] ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 28] ﴿It scorches the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 29] ﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30] ﴿We made the keepers of the Fire none but angels, and We made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain, and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did God intend by this as an example?"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]

**[p. 370]** This surah is Meccan; Ibn 'Atiyya said it is Meccan by consensus. In *al-Tahrir*, Muqatil said: except one verse, which is: ﴿We made their number only a trial﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

Its connection to what precedes it is that the preceding surah contains (*Leave me with the deniers*), and in it is ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]. So it fits with ﴿O you wrapped in your garment! Arise and warn!﴾. Then it mentions the Day of Judgment, and in His words ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11] it mentions some of the deniers.

The majority said: when he was frightened by seeing Gabriel on a chair between heaven and earth, and was terrified of him, he returned to Khadija and said: "Wrap me up, cover me." Then ﴿O you wrapped in your garment!﴾ was revealed. Al-Nakha'i, Qatada and 'A'isha said: he was called while he was in a state of wrapping himself, so he was addressed in one of his states. It is narrated that he had wrapped himself in a *qatifa* (a thick cloth). It was said: he used to hear from Quraysh what he disliked, so he grieved and covered himself with his garment in thought. So he was commanded not to abandon warning them, even if they made him hear and harmed him. 'Ikrima said its meaning: O you who are wrapped for prophethood and its burdens, as He said in *al-Muzzammil*.

Al-Jumhur read *al-muddaththir* with a shaddah on the *dal*. Its origin is *al-mutadaththir*, which was assimilated; it is likewise in the codex of Ubayy in its original form. 'Ikrima read it with a light *dal*, as *al-muzzammil* was read with a light *za'*, meaning: he wrapped himself. Also from 'Ikrima: the *ta'* is vowelled as a passive participle, and he said: "I have wrapped this matter, and it has been bound to you."

﴿Arise and warn!﴾ means: rise from your bed, or *qum* means to begin something, as you say: "Zayd stood up hitting 'Amr," meaning he began. As the poet said:

*Why did the base man begin insulting me?*

Meaning he began. The meaning is: rise with resolve and determination. ﴿And warn!﴾ means: warn of God's punishment and its events. Warning is general to all people, and it is his mission to creation.

﴿And magnify your Lord!﴾ means: glorify His greatness. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Your Lord is singled out for magnifying, which is describing Him with greatness and saying 'God is the Greatest.'" End of quote. This is according to his school, that placing the object before the verb indicates exclusivity. He said: the *fa'* enters for the sense of a condition, as if it were said: "Whatever is, do not neglect glorifying Him." End of quote. This is close to what the grammarians assumed in your saying: *Zaydan fa-idrib* ("Zayd, so strike him"). They said its assumption is: "Be alert, then strike Zayd." So the *fa'* is the answer to the imperative, and this imperative either contains the sense of a condition, or the condition after it is omitted, according to the disagreement among the grammarians about it.

﴿And purify your garments!﴾: The apparent meaning is that he was commanded to purify the garments from impurities, because the purity of garments is a condition for the validity of prayer, and it would be ugly for a believer's garments to be impure. The view that it is literally garments is the view of Ibn Sirin, Ibn Zayd and al-Shafi'i. From this verse al-Shafi'i held that washing impurity from the garment of one praying is obligatory. It was said: its purification is its shortening, and opposing the Arabs in lengthening garments and dragging their trains as a matter of pride and arrogance. The poet said:

*Then they went out, fragrant with musk, sweeping the earth with the fringes of their waist-wraps.*

One is not safe from their being struck by impurity. In a hadith: "The lower garment of the believer reaches to the middle of his shins; there is no blame on him between that and the ankles; what is below that is in the Fire." The majority held that "garments" here is metaphorical. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: its purification is that it not be soiled with filth. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr also said: garments are a metaphor for the heart, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*So take off my garments from your garments.*

Meaning: my heart from your heart. And it is about purity from filth, and he recited the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salama al-Thaqafi:

*Indeed, by the praise of God, I have not put on a treacherous garment, nor do I cover myself with disgrace.*

It was said: it is a metaphor for the purity of deeds, meaning: "And make your deeds righteous." Said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Zayd said: when a man's deeds are evil, they say: "So-and-so has evil garments," and when his deeds are good, they say: "So-and-so has pure garments." Similar to this is from al-Suddi. From this is the poet's saying:

*O God, indeed 'Amir ibn Jahm, or he blamed the pilgrimage in greasy garments.*

Meaning: he soiled it with sins. It was said: garments is a metaphor for the self, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The poet said:

*So I pierced with the long spear his garments.*

Another said:

*The garments of the Banu 'Awf are pure and clean, and their faces are white, clearly bright.*

Meaning: their selves. It was said: garments is a metaphor for the body. Layla said, mentioning camels:

*They threw them with light garments, and we see no likeness of them except the scattered ostriches.*

Meaning: they rode them and threw themselves onto them. It was said: it is a metaphor for the family. God said: ﴿They are garments for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], and purifying oneself with them is choosing chaste believing women. It was said: having intercourse with them in the front passage and not the back, in a state of purity and not during menstruation, related by Ibn Bahr. It was said: it is a metaphor for character, meaning: "And beautify your character." Said by al-Hasan and al-Qurtubi, and from this is his saying:

*Yahya who does not suit evil character, and Yahya the pure of garments, free.*

[p. 372]

That is: good in character. The majority of reciters read ﴿والرِّجْزَ﴾ (*al-rijza*) with a kasra on the rāʾ, which is the dialect of the Quraysh. Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Sulamī, Abū Jaʿfar, Abū Shayba, Ibn Muḥaysin, Ibn Wathhāb, Qatāda, al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-Aʿraj and Ḥafṣ read it with a ḍamma. Some said the two forms have the same meaning, both referring to idols and images. Others said that the kasra refers to separation, shortcomings and immorality, while the ḍamma refers to two idols, Asāf and Nāʾila. ʿIkrima, Mujāhid and al-Zuhrī said it refers to idols in general. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *al-rujz* is wrath, meaning: abandon what leads to it. al-Ḥasan said: it is every act of disobedience, and the meaning of the command is: persist and remain steadfast in abandoning it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was innocent of it. al-Nakhaʿī said: *al-rujz* is sin. al-Qutaybī said: it is punishment, meaning: abandon what leads to it.

The majority read ﴿ولا تَمْنُنْ﴾ (*wa lā tamnun*) with the doubled consonant separated (*fakk al-taḍʿīf*). al-Ḥasan and Abū al-Simmāl read it with the nūn doubled (*shadd al-nūn*). Ibn ʿAbbās and others said: do not give a gift in order to receive more than it. It seems to derive from their saying *manna* when someone gives. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: this is specific to him (ﷺ), and it is permitted for his community, but they will have no reward for it. Also from Ibn ʿAbbās: do not say, "I called, but I was not answered." From Qatāda: do not rely on your deeds. From Ibn Zayd: do not boast of your prophethood, seeking more reward or gain from them. al-Ḥasan said: do not confer favor upon God by your diligence, considering your deeds great and feeling self-admiration because of them. All these statements are forms of *manna*, which is counting and mentioning a favor. Mujāhid said: ﴿ولا تَمْنُنْ تَسْتَكْثِرُ﴾ means: [do not regard as great] what We have burdened you with of the weights of the message, or [do not seek to increase] good. This derives from their saying *ḥablun matīn*, meaning weak. It was also said: do not give to someone while regarding what you give as great and seeing it as much.

The majority read ﴿تَسْتَكْثِرُ﴾ (*tastakthiru*) with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, and the clause is circumstantial (*ḥāliyya*, a clause describing the state of the subject), meaning: seeking more. al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible with the ḍamma that *an* be elided from it and its governing effect be cancelled, as was narrated: *aḥḍuru al-wagha* with a ḍamma. End of his words. This cannot be used to interpret the Qur'an, because such a usage is permitted only in poetry, and we have a sound alternative in the circumstantial reading, meaning: seeking more.

al-Ḥasan and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with a jazm (*jazm*, the absence of final vowel) on the rāʾ. The explanation is that it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿تَمْنُنْ﴾, meaning: do not seek more. This is like His saying ﴿يُضاعَفْ لَهُ العَذابُ﴾ [al-Furqān: 69] in the reading of those who used the jazm, as a substitute for the phrase *yalqa*. And like the poet's saying:

*If you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firewood, thick and coarse, and a fire blazing.*

This would be from the *manna* mentioned in His saying: ﴿لا تُبْطِلُوا صَدَقاتِكم بِالمَنِّ والأذى﴾ [al-Baqara: 264], "Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury," because it is the nature of the one who confers favor to regard what he gives as much and to count it significant. al-Zamakhsharī permitted two possibilities in it: first, that *tastakthiru* be made like *taʿḍudu* and be pronounced with sukūn for lightness; second, that the pause form be considered, so that the connected form follows the pause form. Neither may be used to interpret the Qur'an when there is a stronger reading, namely the substitute.

al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash also read ﴿تَسْتَكْثِرَ﴾ with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, meaning: you will not belittle it. Ibn Masʿūd read ﴿أنْ تَسْتَكْثِرَ﴾ with the particle *an* made explicit.

﴿ولِرَبِّكَ فاصْبِرْ﴾ means: for the sake of your Lord, He commanded him to be patient. This covers patience with the burdens of prophethood, with carrying out obedience to God, and with the harm of the disbelievers. Ibn Zayd said: [be patient] in the face of war with the red and the black, so every matter one is patient in and every matter one is patient from falls within patience. al-Zamakhsharī said: the *fā'* in His saying ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ﴾ indicates causation, as if it were said: be patient with their harm, for before them is a difficult day in which they will meet the consequence of their harm, and you will meet the consequence of your patience with it.

al-Zamakhsharī also said: the *fā'* in (*fa-dhālika*) indicates the response (*jazāʾ*). (If you ask): with what is *idhā* (when) in the accusative? And how is it correct for *yawmiʾidhin* (on that day) to be the adverbial complement of ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾ (a difficult day)? (I answer): *idhā* is in the accusative by what the response clause indicates, because the meaning is: ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ في النّاقُورِ﴾ (when the trumpet is sounded), the matter becomes difficult for the disbelievers. As for the one who permitted *yawmiʾidhin* to be the adverbial complement of ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾, the meaning is: that time of the sounding is the occurrence of a difficult day, because the Day of Resurrection comes and occurs at the moment the trumpet is sounded. It is also permissible for *yawmiʾidhin* to be a built form (*mabnī*) in the nominative position as a substitute for *dhālika*, with ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾ as the predicate, as if it were said: so the Day of the sounding is a difficult day. (If you ask): what is the benefit of His saying ﴿غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ﴾ (not easy), when *ʿasīr* (difficult) would suffice without it? (I answer): when He said ﴿عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾ (upon the disbelievers), restricting the difficulty to them, He said ﴿غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ﴾ to indicate that it is not for them as it is for the believers, an easy and light matter. Thus it combines a threat to the disbelievers with an increase in their rage, and good news and consolation for the believers. It is also permissible that it means a difficulty not expected to become easy, as with the difficulty of worldly affairs that is hoped to become easy. End of his words.

al-Ḥawfī said: ﴿فَإذا﴾ *idhā* is connected to ﴿أنْذِرْ﴾ (warn), meaning: warn them when the trumpet is sounded. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: according to the view of al-Akhfash, *idhā* may be a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with *fa-dhālika* as its predicate and the *fā'* being extra. As for *yawmiʾidhin*, it is an adverbial complement of *dhālika*. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted *ʿalā al-kāfirīn* to be connected to *yasīr*, meaning: not easy upon the disbelievers. It should not be permitted, because it places the object of the governing word (what is attached to *ghayr*) before the governing word itself, which is prohibited according to the sound view, though some permitted it, saying: *anā bi-Zaydin ghayru rāḍin* (I am not content with Zayd).

**[p. 368]** Surah al-Muddaththir (Meccan), fifty-six verses.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿O you wrapped in your garment!﴾ ﴿Arise and warn!﴾ ﴿And magnify your Lord!﴾ ﴿And purify your garments!﴾ ﴿And shun the idol!﴾ ﴿And do not give seeking more.﴾ ﴿And for your Lord, be patient.﴾ ﴿For when the trumpet is sounded,﴾ ﴿that will be a difficult day,﴾ ﴿not easy for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11] ﴿and to whom I gave abundant wealth,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 12] ﴿and sons present with him,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 13] ﴿and whom I made comfortable in every way.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 14] ﴿Then he desires that I should increase him more.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 15] ﴿No! Indeed, he was stubborn toward Our signs.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16] ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep climb.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 17] ﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 18] ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 19] ﴿Then may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 20] ﴿Then he looked.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 21] ﴿Then he frowned and scowled.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 22] ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 23] ﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic, transmitted.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 24] ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 25] ﴿I will burn him in Saqar.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26] ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 27] ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 28] ﴿It scorches the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 29] ﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30] ﴿We made the keepers of the Fire none but angels, and We made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain, and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did God intend by this as an example?" Thus God leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him. And it is nothing but a reminder to the human being.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31] ﴿No! By the moon,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 32] ﴿and by the night when it withdraws,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 33] ﴿and by the morning when it brightens,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 34] ﴿indeed, it is one of the greatest things,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 35] ﴿a warning to the human being,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 36] ﴿to whoever among you wishes to go forward or to lag behind.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 37] ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38] ﴿except the companions of the right,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 39] ﴿in gardens, they ask one another﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 40] ﴿about the criminals:﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 41] ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42] ﴿They will say, "We were not of those who prayed,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43] ﴿and we did not feed the needy,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 44] ﴿and we used to plunge with the plungers,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 45] ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 46] ﴿until the certainty came to us."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 47] ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48] ﴿What is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49] ﴿As if they were startled donkeys﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 50] ﴿fleeing from a lion.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 51] ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 52] ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 53] ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder,﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 54] ﴿so whoever wills may remember it.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 55] ﴿And they will not remember unless God wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 56]

*Tadaththara*: he put on the *didar* (dithar), which is the garment worn over the *shi'ar*. The *shi'ar* is the garment that lies next to the body. From this is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "The Ansar are the *shi'ar* (inner garment), and the people are the *didar* (outer garment)."

*Al-naqr*: the sound. The poet said:

*I lower it with the naqr when I have mounted it, and it raises a gaze that is not hidden, lowered.*

And the rajaz poet said:

*I am the son of Mawiyya, when the naqr became intense.*

He means *al-naqr*, and he transferred the vowel. So *al-naqur* is *fa'ul* from it, like *al-jasus* derived from *al-tajassus*.

*Abasa* (yaabisu, *abs*, *ubus*): he frowned. *Al-abs* is what clings to the tails of camels of their dung and urine. Abu al-Najm said:

*As if on their tails were the young camels, from the dung of the summer, the horns of the gazelles.*

*Basar*: he gathered what is between his eyes, and his face became pale. He said:

*We accompanied Tamim on the morning of al-Jifar, with a dark, blameworthy, scowling (bāsira) grey horse.*

The people of Yemen say: *basara al-markab* and *absara* when the ship stopped, and we have *absarna*. The Arabs say: "a scowling face, clearly scowling," when it changed and blackened.

*Lahahu al-basr*: it changed his form. He said:

*She says, "What has changed you, traveller? O daughter of my uncle, the heat has changed me."*

Another said:

*Hind wonders if she sees me pale, saying to something the hot winds have scorched.*

Al-Akhfash said: *al-luh* is the intensity of thirst. *Lahahu al-atash* and *lawwahahu* mean it changed him. The poet said:

*She gave me a drink of water on a pale, dry tongue, may God give it abundant, flowing rain.*

It is said: *iltah*, meaning he became thirsty.

*Al-qaswara*: the archers and hunters, said by Ibn Kaysan. Or the lion, said by a group of lexicographers. He said:

*A hidden one the heroes pursue, as if he were a lion, a fierce tiger.*

Or the strong men. Labid said:

*When we shout a shout in our assembly, the men who hunt come to us, the hunters.*

Or the darkness of the beginning of the night, not the darkness of its end, said by Ibn al-A'rabi and Tha'lab.
