It is also reported from him *tis'atun wa 'ashr* with a damma, and he converted the hamza in *a'shur* into a pure waw for lightness, and the ba' in both is marked with a construction damma, because it alternates with the fatha, to avoid joining five vowels in one direction. From Sulayman ibn Qunna, the brother of Ibrahim, it is reported that he read *tis'atu a'shurin* with a damma on the ta' as an inflectional damma, and its being annexed to *a'shurin*, and *a'shurin* is genitive and nunated; this is on the basis of unpacking the compound. The author of *al-Lawami'h* said: and according to this reading, which is the reading of one who reads *a'shurin* as indeclinable or inflected insofar as it is a plural, it follows that the angels who are over the Fire are ninety angels. End. There is some abridgement in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It has also been read *tis'atu a'shurin*, the plural of *'asir*, like *yamin* and *ayman*. End.

This Sulayman ibn Qunna is the one who praised the family of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he is the one who said:

*I passed by the dwellings of the family of Muhammad,*
*and I did not see their like on the day they dismounted.*
*They were a support, then they became a calamity;*
*indeed those calamities have grown great and immense.*

﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire but angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], meaning: We made them a creation against which no one among the people has any power. ﴿And We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], meaning: a cause of trial. ﴿A trial﴾ is the second object of *ja'alna* (We made), meaning: We made that number, which is nineteen, a cause of trial for the disbelievers. So ﴿a trial﴾ is not an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). Their trial is that they showed their defiance in their opposition, and that was by way of mockery, for they deny the Resurrection, the Fire and its guardians.

﴿So that they may be certain﴾ (*li-yastayqina*): this is an object of purpose, and it is connected to *ja'alna*, not to *fitna*. So the trial is not caused by certainty; rather the caused element is that making the number a cause for *fitna* [for] ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, and they are the Jews and the Christians, [who are certain] that this Qur'an is from God, since they find this number in their revealed books, and they know that the Messenger did not read it, nor did anyone read it to him, but his Book confirms the books of the prophets, since all of that is truth that supports one another from God Most High. This meaning was stated by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. By the arrival of the realities from God Most High, every person of faith increases in faith, and doubt is removed from those among the People of the Book who affirm, and from the believers.

It is said: the number became a trial only because they mock and say, "Why were they not twenty? And what requires that this number be specified for existence?" They say: this small number, by punishing the majority of the world of jinn and humans from the first of God's creation until the Hour is established, is strong.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: he made the disbelievers' being tested by the number of the guardians a cause for the certainty of the People of the Book and the increase of faith of the believers and the mockery of the disbelievers and the hypocrites, so what is the correct way of understanding that?" I answer: He did not make their being tested by the number the cause of that; rather the number itself is what was made the cause. That is because what is meant by His saying, ﴿And We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], is: "And We have not made their number but nineteen." So he placed ﴿a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ in the position of *nineteen*, because the state of this number, lacking one from the decade of twenty, is that whoever does not believe in God and His wisdom will be tested by it, and will object, mock, and not submit with the submission of a believer, even if the wisdom behind it is hidden from him. It is as if it were said: "We have made their number a number whose nature is that it tests, in order to make the believers certain and the disbelievers bewildered." End. This is a strange question and an answer in which there is distortion of the Book of God Most High, for he claimed that the meaning of ﴿but as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ is: "but nineteen." No sensible person, nor anyone with the least intelligence, would go to this. Sufficient as a refutation of it is the distortion of the Book of God and the placing of words different from [its] words and a meaning different from [its] meaning.

It is said: *li-yastayqina* is connected to a hidden verb, meaning: "We did that so that they may be certain."

﴿And that they may not doubt﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31]: this is an emphasis on His saying *li-yastayqina*, since affirming certainty and negating doubt is more eloquent and more emphatic in description, for the complete tranquility of the soul.

As for ﴿and those in whose hearts is a sickness﴾: al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: the surah is Meccan, and there was no hypocrisy in Mecca; the sickness in the verse is rather agitation and weakness of faith. It is also said: it is a report of the unseen, meaning: and that the hypocrites, who will plot in the future time in Medina after the Hijra, may say: ﴿What did God intend by this as a parable?﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31]. When they heard this number, they were not guided and were bewildered, so some of them asked others about it, considering it far-fetched that this could be from God; they called it a "parable" (*mathal*) metaphorically, from the parable that is struck, out of astonishment at this number. The meaning is: "What did God intend by this wondrous number?" Their intention was to deny its very origin, and that it is not from God. The grammatical analysis of such a sentence has been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 74, verse 11–30 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾: There is no disagreement that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. It is narrated that he was nicknamed "al-Wahid" (the Unique), meaning because he had no equal in his wealth and in the honour of his household. The apparent reading is that "wahidan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the omitted pronoun referring back to "man", meaning: I created him solitary, humble, and poor, with neither wealth nor children, and then God the Exalted gave him wealth and children, but he denied His blessing, associated partners with Him, and mocked His religion. It has also been said: it is a circumstantial qualifier of the object pronoun in "dharni" (leave me), as Mujahid said, meaning: leave me alone with him, for I will requite you in taking vengeance upon him. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier of the "ta" in "khalaqtu" (I created), meaning: I created him alone, none shared with Me in My creation, so I will destroy him, and I do not need a helper in destroying him. It has also been said: "wahidan" means one whose father is not known. Al-Walid was known to be an illegitimate child (da'iyy), as was mentioned earlier in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Cruel, and after that, of doubtful lineage﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]. If he was called "wahid," it cannot be that it is in the accusative as a form of dispraise, because God the Exalted would not confirm him in that he is unique with no equal. This was refuted by saying that when he was given that title it became a proper name (alam), and a proper name does not convey a descriptive attribute in the one named; and also it is possible to interpret it as meaning he was unique in disbelief, wickedness, and baseness.

﴿And to him I granted extensive wealth﴾: Ibn Abbas said: he had between Mecca and al-Ta'if camels, cultivated land, cattle, gardens, male slaves, and female slaves. It has been said: he was a possessor of crops, livestock, and trade. Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said: "al-mal al-mamdud" is land, because it is extended (muddat). Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the rent-income earned monthly, so it is an extension in time that does not cease. It has been said: it is a specific amount, and they differed in specifying it. Among what was said: a thousand dinars; it was said: a thousand thousand dinars; and all of this is arbitrary.

﴿And sons attending him﴾: meaning present with him in Mecca, not leaving him because of their wealth, so he is at ease with them; or "shuhudan" means men who attend with him the gatherings and assemblies, or whose testimony is heard in matters that are adjudicated. There was disagreement about their number. Among those mentioned are Khalid, Hisham, and Imara, who embraced Islam, and al-Walid, al-As, Qays, and Abd Shams. Muqatil said: after this verse and its revelation, al-Walid continued in decline in his wealth and his children until he died.

﴿And I made preparation for him, a [full] preparation﴾: meaning I smoothed the way, prepared, and spread out for him a carpet, until he settled in his town, at peace, whose opinion is consulted. Ibn Abbas said: I broadened for him what lies between Yemen and Syria. Mujahid said: I prepared for him wealth, one part upon another, as a bed is prepared.

﴿Then he desires that I should add more﴾: meaning beyond what I have given him of wealth and children. (Kalla) meaning: it will not be so, given his denial of the blessings. Al-Hasan and others said: "Then he desires that I should admit him to Paradise," because he used to say: if Muhammad is truthful, Paradise was created only for me.

﴿Then he desires﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an expression of astonishment at his desire and a denunciation, meaning: there is no increase beyond what he was given in abundance and expanse. (Kalla): a cutting off of his hope and a rebuke. End. His desire for more is evidence of his greed and love of the world.

﴿Indeed, he was obstinate toward Our signs﴾: this is a reason for the rebuke, in the form of a resumptive clause, as if someone said: why is he not given more? So it was said: he was obstinate toward the signs of the Benefactor and disbelieved thereby, and the disbeliever does not deserve more. The signs are attributed to the blessings because of the connection with His words: ﴿And I granted him extensive wealth﴾ up to the end of what God gave him. It is best to interpret it as referring to the verses of the Qur'an, because of his speech concerning it in the Qur'an and his claim that it is sorcery. (Sa-urhiquhu) meaning: I will burden him and distress him with hardship and difficulty; (sa'ud): a steep ascent in Hell, whenever something of a human is placed upon it, it melts and then returns. The word "sa'ud" in the language means a difficult ascent. The explanation of "ʿanid" has already been given in Surah Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated﴾: It is narrated that al-Walid debated Abu Jahl and a group of Quraysh concerning the matter of the Qur'an, and said: Indeed it has sweetness, its lower part is abundant, its branch is fruitful, it crushes what is beneath it, and it rises and nothing rises above it; and similar words. They opposed him and said: it is poetry. He said: By God, it is not poetry; we know poetry in its rhythmic and its measured forms. They said: then it is a soothsaying. He said: By God, it is not soothsaying; we have seen soothsayers. They said: he is a madman. He said: By God, he is not a madman; we have seen the madman and his choking. They said: it is sorcery. He said: As for this, it resembles sorcery, and he speaks words of his own. This was narrated with wordings other than these, close in meaning, and in it: "And you claim that he is a liar; have you tested him in any lie?" They said: "In all of that, no, by God." Then they said: "Then what is it?" So he reflected and then said: "It is nothing but a sorcerer. Have you not seen him separating a man from his wife, his child, and his clients? And what he says is nothing but sorcery transmitted from the likes of Musaylima and the people of Babylon." The assembly erupted in joy and they dispersed, astonished at him. It is also narrated that al-Walid heard from the Qur'an what pleased him and praised it, then heard it again many times, until he nearly approached Islam. He entered upon Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, several times. Then Abu Jahl came to him and said: "O Walid! Are you aware that Quraysh has blamed you for your entering upon the son of Abu Quhafa, and they claim that you only intend to eat his food? They have hated you for your closeness to the matter of Muhammad, and what will save you among them is only that you say a statement in this matter that pleases them." Abu Jahl tempted him and he was tempted, and said: "I will do it."

﴿Indeed, he reflected﴾: a reason for the threat in His words: ﴿I will burden him with a steep ascent﴾. It has been said: it is also permissible that ﴿Indeed, he reflected﴾ is a substitute for His words: ﴿Indeed, he was obstinate toward Our signs﴾, clarifying the reality of his obstinacy. "Fakkara" meaning: about the Qur'an and the one who brought it; "wa-qaddara" meaning: within himself, what he would say about it.

﴿So he was destroyed; how he calculated﴾: It has been said: "qutila" means "lu'ina" (cursed). It has been said: "ghulib" (overcome) and "quhira" (subdued). That is from the verse of the poet:

"For your two arrows in the depths of a slain heart"

meaning: humbled and subdued by love. So "lu'ina" is a curse upon him for expulsion and distance, and "ghulib" is a report of his subjugation and humiliation. And "kayfa qaddara" means: how he calculated what it is not valid to calculate and what no rational person may suitably calculate? It has been said: it is a supplication whose implication is approval and wonder. It was said that this is because of his earlier stance of praising the Qur'an and denying poetry, soothsaying, and madness from it, so it runs in the manner of the saying of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: "May God fight Kuthayyir," as if he saw us when he said such and such. It has been said: that is for his hitting upon what Quraysh sought from him. It has been said: that is praise of him in the manner of mockery. It has been said: that is a recounting of what they repeated of their saying: "He was destroyed, how he calculated," mocking them and their admiration of his calculation and their magnifying of his words, and this is far-fetched. The saying of the Arabs, "qatalahumu Allah" (may God fight them), is well known as said when magnifying a matter and wondering at it, and its meaning is that he has reached a level for which he is envied and for which his enemies invoke a curse upon him. The interrogative in "kayfa qaddara" carries the sense of: how wondrous his calculation is and how strange it is, like the saying "ayyu rajulin Zayd?" meaning: how great he is. The repetition with "thumma" was to indicate that the second is more emphatic than the first because of the interval between them; as if He cursed him first, hoping he would desist from what he was intending, but he did not, so He cursed him a second time. ﴿Then he looked﴾ meaning: he reflected a second time. It has been said: he looked at the faces of the people. ﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾ meaning: he knitted his brow and grimaced when the means were narrowed upon him and he did not know what to say. It has been said: he frowned in the face of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ. ﴿Then he turned away﴾: he returned turning his back. It has been said: he turned away from the truth. ﴿And he was arrogant﴾: it has been said: he became haughty and arrogant; it has been said: he was arrogant toward the truth. He described him with the states by which he was distinguished when he wanted to say: what he said, all of it, was by way of mockery, and that what he said was a lie and fabrication, for if it were possible, he would have had other states than these, such as joy of heart and visible delight, gladness and cheerfulness in his face; and if it were true, he would not have needed this reflection, for the truth is clear and manifests itself without any laboring of thought or delay of reflection. Do you not see that man and his saying when he saw the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ: "I knew that his face is not the face of a liar," and he embraced Islam immediately. It has been said: "Then he looked" means he looked at what he could argue for the Qur'an, and saw what is in it of inimitability and of the announcement of the rank of the Messenger, ﷺ, and his looking in that continued.

﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾: indicating his deliberation and slowness in his reflection, since between these there is delay and distance. The conjunction in "wa-basar" and in "wa-istakbar" is with "waw" because "basr" is close to "ʿabs" (frowning), so it is as if, by way of emphasis and arrogance, it appears that it is a cause of turning away, since arrogance is a meaning in the heart, while turning away is a physical act; so they are cause and effect, and therefore they are not joined by "thumma". He mentioned the effect before the cause because it is what is apparent to the eye, and the conjunction with "waw" suited it. The conjunction in "fa-qala" is with "fa" to indicate immediacy, because when this statement came to his mind after his search, he could not restrain himself from uttering it without delay. The meaning of "yu'thar": it is transmitted and narrated. The poet said:

"I would have said of speech what would always be transmitted from me by the one who narrates."

It has been said: "yu'thar" means it is chosen and preferred over other kinds of sorcery, so it is from "iithar" (preference), and the meaning of "illa sihr" is: resembling sorcery.

﴿This is nothing but the speech of a human being﴾: a confirmation of what precedes it, meaning: it is gathered from the speech of people, and it appears that the disbelief of al-Walid was nothing but obstinacy. Do you not see his praise of the Qur'an, and his denial of all that they attributed to it of poetry, soothsaying, and madness; and his story with the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, when he recited to him the opening of Surah Fussilat up to His words: ﴿But if they turn away, say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13], and how he adjured him by kinship to be silent? ﴿I will drive him into Saqar﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: it is a substitute for ﴿I will burden him with a steep ascent﴾. End. It appears that they are two sentences, each following the other, so He threatened, by way of warning, the disobedience that preceded each of them: He threatened for being obstinate toward the signs of God with a burdensome ascent, and for his saying that the Qur'an is sorcery that is transmitted, with being driven into Saqar. The discussion of Saqar has already been given at the end of Surah al-Qamar.

﴿And what can make you know what Saqar is?﴾: magnification of its terror and severity. ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾: meaning it does not spare anyone cast into it, and it leaves no degree of punishment without bringing it to him.

﴿Scorching the human being﴾: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Razin, and the majority said: it means changing the complexion, burning the skins and blackening them; "al-bashar" is the plural of "bashara" (skin), and the Arabs say: "lahat al-nar al-shay'" (the fire scorched the thing) when it burns it and blackens it. Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: "lawwahah" is an intensive form from "laha" (to appear), and the meaning is that it appears to the people, that is, humankind, from a distance of five hundred years, and that is because of its greatness, its terror, and its deterrence, as in His words: ﴿You shall surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur: 6], and His words: ﴿And Hell is made manifest to whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. The majority read "lawwahatun" in the nominative, meaning: it is scorching. Al-Awfi, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Hasan, and Ibn Abi Abla read "liwahatan" in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial qualifier, because the fire that leaves nothing and spares nothing can only be changing the complexions. Al-Zamakhshari said: in the accusative by way of specification for the sake of terrifying.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 74, verses 11–30 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿Over it are nineteen﴾: The specification (*tamyiz*, the noun that clarifies a number) is omitted, and what comes to mind is that it refers to angels. Do you not see that the Arabs, who were eloquent, understood from it that the meaning was angels when they heard this? Abu Jahl said to the Quraysh: "May your mothers be bereaved! Do I hear that Ibn Abi Kabsha is telling you that the guardians of the Fire are nineteen, while you are the numerous ones? Can not each ten of you overpower one man among them?" Abu al-Ashadd ibn Usayd ibn Kalda al-Jumahi, who was very strong, said: "I will suffice you for seventeen, so suffice me for two."

Then God Most High revealed: ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire but angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], meaning: We have not made them men of your kind who can be overpowered. And God Most High revealed concerning Abu Jahl: ﴿Woe to you, and woe﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:34].

It is said that the omitted specification is a category of angels, and it is said that it is "chiefs" (*naqib*). The meaning of ﴿over it﴾ is that they are in charge of its affairs, and to them belongs the assembling of its guardians (*zabaniyya*). What appears from the number, from the verse that follows it, and from the hadith, is that these are the chiefs (*nuqaba'*). Do you not see God's saying: ﴿None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], and the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace (ﷺ): "On that Day Hell will be brought, and it will have seventy thousand bridles, and with each bridle seventy thousand angels who will drag it"?

The exegetes have mentioned some attributes of these angels, their creation and their strength, and the acts God has made them capable of, of which only God knows the soundness. Likewise Abu Abd Allah al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned a ruling, according to his own assumption, concerning these angels being of this specific number, which may be consulted in his tafsir.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿tis'ata 'ashara﴾ with both parts built on fatha, according to the well-known usage of the language for this number. Abu Ja'far and Talha ibn Sulayman read it with the 'ayn sukun, disliking the succession of vowels. Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Qutayb and Ibrahim ibn Qunna read it with a damma on the ta' (*tā'*), which is a vowel of construction (*harakat bina'*) turned to instead of fatha, to avoid the succession of five fathas. It should not be supposed that it is a vowel of inflection (*harakat i'rab*), because if it were a vowel of inflection, then ('ashara) would be inflected.

Anas also read *tis'atu* with a damma and *a'shur* with a fatha. The author of *al-Lawami'h* said: it is possible that he made the plural of *'ashara* into *a'shur*, then treated it like *tis'ata 'ashara*. It is also reported from him *tis'atun wa 'ashr* with a damma, and he converted the hamza in *a'shur* into a pure waw for lightness, and the ba' in both is marked with a construction damma, because it alternates with the fatha, to avoid joining five vowels in one direction. From Sulayman ibn Qunna, the brother of Ibrahim, it is reported that he read *tis'atu a'shurin* with a damma on the ta' as an inflectional damma, and its being annexed to *a'shurin*, and *a'shurin* is genitive and nunated; this is on the basis of unpacking the compound. The author of *al-Lawami'h* said: and according to this reading, which is the reading of one who reads *a'shurin* as indeclinable or inflected insofar as it is a plural, it follows that the angels who are over the Fire are ninety angels. End. There is some abridgement in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It has also been read *tis'atu a'shurin*, the plural of *'asir*, like *yamin* and *ayman*. End.

This Sulayman ibn Qunna is the one who praised the family of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he is the one who said:

*I passed by the dwellings of the family of Muhammad,*
*and I did not see their like on the day they dismounted.*
*They were a support, then they became a calamity;*
*indeed those calamities have grown great and immense.*

﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire but angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], meaning: We made them a creation against which no one among the people has any power. ﴿And We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], meaning: a cause of trial. ﴿A trial﴾ is the second object of *ja'alna* (We made), meaning: We made that number, which is nineteen, a cause of trial for the disbelievers. Their trial is that they showed their defiance in their opposition, and that was by way of mockery, for they deny the Resurrection, the Fire and its guardians.

﴿So that they may be certain﴾ (*li-yastayqina*): this is an object of purpose, and it is connected to *ja'alna*, not to *fitna*. So the trial is not caused by certainty; rather the caused element is that making the number a cause for *fitna* [for] ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, and they are the Jews and the Christians, [who are certain] that this Qur'an is from God, since they find this number in their revealed books, and they know that the Messenger did not read it, nor did anyone read it to him, but his Book confirms the books of the prophets, since all of that is truth that supports one another from God Most High. They say: this small number, by punishing the majority of the world of jinn and humans from the first of God's creation until the Hour is established, is strong.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: he made the disbelievers' being tested by the number of the guardians a cause for the certainty of the People of the Book and the increase of faith of the believers and the mockery of the disbelievers and the hypocrites, so what is the correct way of understanding that?" I answer: He did not make their being tested by the number the cause of that; rather the number itself is what was made the cause. That is because what is meant by His saying, ﴿And We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], is: "And We have not made their number but nineteen." Sufficient as a refutation of it is the distortion of the Book of God and the placing of words different from [its] words and a meaning different from [its] meaning.

It is said: *li-yastayqina* is connected to a hidden verb, meaning: "We did that so that they may be certain."

﴿And that they may not doubt﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31]: this is an emphasis on His saying *li-yastayqina*, since affirming certainty and negating doubt is more eloquent and more emphatic in description, for the complete tranquility of the soul.

When they heard this number, they were not guided and were bewildered, so some of them asked others about it, considering it far-fetched that this could be from God; they called it a "parable" (*mathal*) metaphorically, from the parable that is struck, out of astonishment at this number. The meaning is: "What did God intend by this wondrous number?" Their intention was to deny its very origin, and that it is not from God. The grammatical analysis of such a sentence has been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 74, verse 11–30 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾: There is no disagreement that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. It is narrated that he was nicknamed "al-Wahid" (the Unique), meaning because he had no equal in his wealth and in the honour of his household. The apparent reading is that "wahidan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the omitted pronoun referring back to "man", meaning: I created him solitary, humble, and poor, with neither wealth nor children, and then God the Exalted gave him wealth and children, but he denied His blessing, associated partners with Him, and mocked His religion. It has also been said: it is a circumstantial qualifier of the object pronoun in "dharni" (leave me), as Mujahid said, meaning: leave me alone with him, for I will requite you in taking vengeance upon him. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier of the "ta" in "khalaqtu" (I created), meaning: I created him alone, none shared with Me in My creation, so I will destroy him, and I do not need a helper in destroying him. It has also been said: "wahidan" means one whose father is not known. Al-Walid was known to be an illegitimate child (da'iyy), as was mentioned earlier in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Cruel, and after that, of doubtful lineage﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]. If he was called "wahid," it cannot be that it is in the accusative as a form of dispraise, because God the Exalted would not confirm him in that he is unique with no equal. This was refuted by saying that when he was given that title it became a proper name (alam), and a proper name does not convey a descriptive attribute in the one named; and also it is possible to interpret it as meaning he was unique in disbelief, wickedness, and baseness.

﴿And to him I granted extensive wealth﴾: Ibn Abbas said: he had between Mecca and al-Ta'if camels, cultivated land, cattle, gardens, male slaves, and female slaves. It has been said: he was a possessor of crops, livestock, and trade. Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said: "al-mal al-mamdud" is land, because it is extended (muddat). Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the rent-income earned monthly, so it is an extension in time that does not cease. It has been said: it is a specific amount, and they differed in specifying it. Among what was said: a thousand dinars; it was said: a thousand thousand dinars; and all of this is arbitrary.

﴿And sons attending him﴾: meaning present with him in Mecca, not leaving him because of their wealth, so he is at ease with them; or "shuhudan" means men who attend with him the gatherings and assemblies, or whose testimony is heard in matters that are adjudicated. There was disagreement about their number. Among those mentioned are Khalid, Hisham, and Imara, who embraced Islam, and al-Walid, al-As, Qays, and Abd Shams. Muqatil said: after this verse and its revelation, al-Walid continued in decline in his wealth and his children until he died.

﴿And I made preparation for him, a [full] preparation﴾: meaning I smoothed the way, prepared, and spread out for him a carpet, until he settled in his town, at peace, whose opinion is consulted. Ibn Abbas said: I broadened for him what lies between Yemen and Syria. Mujahid said: I prepared for him wealth, one part upon another, as a bed is prepared.

﴿Then he desires that I should add more﴾: meaning beyond what I have given him of wealth and children. (Kalla) meaning: it will not be so, given his denial of the blessings. Al-Hasan and others said: "Then he desires that I should admit him to Paradise," because he used to say: if Muhammad is truthful, Paradise was created only for me.

﴿Then he desires﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an expression of astonishment at his desire and a denunciation, meaning: there is no increase beyond what he was given in abundance and expanse. (Kalla): a cutting off of his hope and a rebuke. End. His desire for more is evidence of his greed and love of the world.

﴿Indeed, he was obstinate toward Our signs﴾: this is a reason for the rebuke, in the form of a resumptive clause, as if someone said: why is he not given more? So it was said: he was obstinate toward the signs of the Benefactor and disbelieved thereby, and the disbeliever does not deserve more. The signs are attributed to the blessings because of the connection with His words: ﴿And I granted him extensive wealth﴾ up to the end of what God gave him. It is best to interpret it as referring to the verses of the Qur'an, because of his speech concerning it in the Qur'an and his claim that it is sorcery. (Sa-urhiquhu) meaning: I will burden him and distress him with hardship and difficulty; (sa'ud): a steep ascent in Hell, whenever something of a human is placed upon it, it melts and then returns. The word "sa'ud" in the language means a difficult ascent. The explanation of "ʿanid" has already been given in Surah Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated﴾: It is narrated that al-Walid debated Abu Jahl and a group of Quraysh concerning the matter of the Qur'an, and said: Indeed it has sweetness, its lower part is abundant, its branch is fruitful, it crushes what is beneath it, and it rises and nothing rises above it; and similar words. They opposed him and said: it is poetry. He said: By God, it is not poetry; we know poetry in its rhythmic and its measured forms. They said: then it is a soothsaying. He said: By God, it is not soothsaying; we have seen soothsayers. They said: he is a madman. He said: By God, he is not a madman; we have seen the madman and his choking. They said: it is sorcery. He said: As for this, it resembles sorcery, and he speaks words of his own. This was narrated with wordings other than these, close in meaning, and in it: "And you claim that he is a liar; have you tested him in any lie?" They said: "In all of that, no, by God." Then they said: "Then what is it?" So he reflected and then said: "It is nothing but a sorcerer. Have you not seen him separating a man from his wife, his child, and his clients? And what he says is nothing but sorcery transmitted from the likes of Musaylima and the people of Babylon." The assembly erupted in joy and they dispersed, astonished at him. It is also narrated that al-Walid heard from the Qur'an what pleased him and praised it, then heard it again many times, until he nearly approached Islam. He entered upon Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, several times. Then Abu Jahl came to him and said: "O Walid! Are you aware that Quraysh has blamed you for your entering upon the son of Abu Quhafa, and they claim that you only intend to eat his food? They have hated you for your closeness to the matter of Muhammad, and what will save you among them is only that you say a statement in this matter that pleases them." Abu Jahl tempted him and he was tempted, and said: "I will do it."

﴿Indeed, he reflected﴾: a reason for the threat in His words: ﴿I will burden him with a steep ascent﴾. It has been said: it is also permissible that ﴿Indeed, he reflected﴾ is a substitute for His words: ﴿Indeed, he was obstinate toward Our signs﴾, clarifying the reality of his obstinacy. "Fakkara" meaning: about the Qur'an and the one who brought it; "wa-qaddara" meaning: within himself, what he would say about it.

﴿So he was destroyed; how he calculated﴾: It has been said: "qutila" means "lu'ina" (cursed). It has been said: "ghulib" (overcome) and "quhira" (subdued). That is from the verse of the poet:

"For your two arrows in the depths of a slain heart"

meaning: humbled and subdued by love. So "lu'ina" is a curse upon him for expulsion and distance, and "ghulib" is a report of his subjugation and humiliation. And "kayfa qaddara" means: how he calculated what it is not valid to calculate and what no rational person may suitably calculate? It has been said: it is a supplication whose implication is approval and wonder. It was said that this is because of his earlier stance of praising the Qur'an and denying poetry, soothsaying, and madness from it, so it runs in the manner of the saying of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: "May God fight Kuthayyir," as if he saw us when he said such and such. It has been said: that is for his hitting upon what Quraysh sought from him. It has been said: that is praise of him in the manner of mockery. It has been said: that is a recounting of what they repeated of their saying: "He was destroyed, how he calculated," mocking them and their admiration of his calculation and their magnifying of his words, and this is far-fetched. The saying of the Arabs, "qatalahumu Allah" (may God fight them), is well known as said when magnifying a matter and wondering at it, and its meaning is that he has reached a level for which he is envied and for which his enemies invoke a curse upon him. The interrogative in "kayfa qaddara" carries the sense of: how wondrous his calculation is and how strange it is, like the saying "ayyu rajulin Zayd?" meaning: how great he is. The repetition with "thumma" was to indicate that the second is more emphatic than the first because of the interval between them; as if He cursed him first, hoping he would desist from what he was intending, but he did not, so He cursed him a second time. ﴿Then he looked﴾ meaning: he reflected a second time. It has been said: he looked at the faces of the people. ﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾ meaning: he knitted his brow and grimaced when the means were narrowed upon him and he did not know what to say. It has been said: he frowned in the face of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ. ﴿Then he turned away﴾: he returned turning his back. It has been said: he turned away from the truth. ﴿And he was arrogant﴾: it has been said: he became haughty and arrogant; it has been said: he was arrogant toward the truth. He described him with the states by which he was distinguished when he wanted to say: what he said, all of it, was by way of mockery, and that what he said was a lie and fabrication, for if it were possible, he would have had other states than these, such as joy of heart and visible delight, gladness and cheerfulness in his face; and if it were true, he would not have needed this reflection, for the truth is clear and manifests itself without any laboring of thought or delay of reflection. Do you not see that man and his saying when he saw the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ: "I knew that his face is not the face of a liar," and he embraced Islam immediately. It has been said: "Then he looked" means he looked at what he could argue for the Qur'an, and saw what is in it of inimitability and of the announcement of the rank of the Messenger, ﷺ, and his looking in that continued.

﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾: indicating his deliberation and slowness in his reflection, since between these there is delay and distance. The conjunction in "wa-basar" and in "wa-istakbar" is with "waw" because "basr" is close to "ʿabs" (frowning), so it is as if, by way of emphasis and arrogance, it appears that it is a cause of turning away, since arrogance is a meaning in the heart, while turning away is a physical act; so they are cause and effect, and therefore they are not joined by "thumma". He mentioned the effect before the cause because it is what is apparent to the eye, and the conjunction with "waw" suited it. The conjunction in "fa-qala" is with "fa" to indicate immediacy, because when this statement came to his mind after his search, he could not restrain himself from uttering it without delay. The meaning of "yu'thar": it is transmitted and narrated. The poet said:

"I would have said of speech what would always be transmitted from me by the one who narrates."

It has been said: "yu'thar" means it is chosen and preferred over other kinds of sorcery, so it is from "iithar" (preference), and the meaning of "illa sihr" is: resembling sorcery.

﴿This is nothing but the speech of a human being﴾: a confirmation of what precedes it, meaning: it is gathered from the speech of people, and it appears that the disbelief of al-Walid was nothing but obstinacy. Do you not see his praise of the Qur'an, and his denial of all that they attributed to it of poetry, soothsaying, and madness; and his story with the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, when he recited to him the opening of Surah Fussilat up to His words: ﴿But if they turn away, say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13], and how he adjured him by kinship to be silent? ﴿I will drive him into Saqar﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: it is a substitute for ﴿I will burden him with a steep ascent﴾. End. It appears that they are two sentences, each following the other, so He threatened, by way of warning, the disobedience that preceded each of them: He threatened for being obstinate toward the signs of God with a burdensome ascent, and for his saying that the Qur'an is sorcery that is transmitted, with being driven into Saqar. The discussion of Saqar has already been given at the end of Surah al-Qamar.

﴿And what can make you know what Saqar is?﴾: magnification of its terror and severity. ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾: meaning it does not spare anyone cast into it, and it leaves no degree of punishment without bringing it to him.

﴿Scorching the human being﴾: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Razin, and the majority said: it means changing the complexion, burning the skins and blackening them; "al-bashar" is the plural of "bashara" (skin), and the Arabs say: "lahat al-nar al-shay'" (the fire scorched the thing) when it burns it and blackens it. Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: "lawwahah" is an intensive form from "laha" (to appear), and the meaning is that it appears to the people, that is, humankind, from a distance of five hundred years, and that is because of its greatness, its terror, and its deterrence, as in His words: ﴿You shall surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur: 6], and His words: ﴿And Hell is made manifest to whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. The majority read "lawwahatun" in the nominative, meaning: it is scorching. Al-Awfi, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Hasan, and Ibn Abi Abla read "liwahatan" in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial qualifier, because the fire that leaves nothing and spares nothing can only be changing the complexions. Al-Zamakhshari said: in the accusative by way of specification for the sake of terrifying.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 74, verses 11–30 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿Over it are nineteen﴾: The specification (*tamyiz*, the noun that clarifies a number) is omitted, and what comes to mind is that it refers to angels. Do you not see that the Arabs, who were eloquent, understood from it that the meaning was angels when they heard this? Abu Jahl said to the Quraysh: "May your mothers be bereaved! Do I hear that Ibn Abi Kabsha is telling you that the guardians of the Fire are nineteen, while you are the numerous ones? Can not each ten of you overpower one man among them?" Abu al-Ashadd ibn Usayd ibn Kalda al-Jumahi, who was very strong, said: "I will suffice you for seventeen, so suffice me for two."

Then God Most High revealed: ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire but angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], meaning: We have not made them men of your kind who can be overpowered. And God Most High revealed concerning Abu Jahl: ﴿Woe to you, and woe﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:34].

It is said that the omitted specification is a category of angels, and it is said that it is "chiefs" (*naqib*). The meaning of ﴿over it﴾ is that they are in charge of its affairs, and to them belongs the assembling of its guardians (*zabaniyya*). What appears from the number, from the verse that follows it, and from the hadith, is that these are the chiefs (*nuqaba'*). Do you not see God's saying: ﴿None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], and the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace (ﷺ): "On that Day Hell will be brought, and it will have seventy thousand bridles, and with each bridle seventy thousand angels who will drag it"?

The exegetes have mentioned some attributes of these angels, their creation and their strength, and the acts God has made them capable of, of which only God knows the soundness. Likewise Abu Abd Allah al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned a ruling, according to his own assumption, concerning these angels being of this specific number, which may be consulted in his tafsir.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿tis'ata 'ashara﴾ with both parts built on fatha, according to the well-known usage of the language for this number. Abu Ja'far and Talha ibn Sulayman read it with the 'ayn sukun, disliking the succession of vowels. Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Qutayb and Ibrahim ibn Qunna read it with a damma on the ta' (*tā'*), which is a vowel of construction (*harakat bina'*) turned to instead of fatha, to avoid the succession of five fathas. It should not be supposed that it is a vowel of inflection (*harakat i'rab*), because if it were a vowel of inflection, then ('ashara) would be inflected.

Anas also read *tis'atu* with a damma and *a'shur* with a fatha. The author of *al-Lawami'h* said: it is possible that he made the plural of *'ashara* into *a'shur*, then treated it like *tis'ata 'ashara*. It is also reported from him *tis'atun wa 'ashr* with a damma, and he converted the hamza in *a'shur* into a pure waw for lightness, and the ba' in both is marked with a construction damma, because it alternates with the fatha, to avoid joining five vowels in one direction. From Sulayman ibn Qunna, the brother of Ibrahim, it is reported that he read *tis'atu a'shurin* with a damma on the ta' as an inflectional damma, and its being annexed to *a'shurin*, and *a'shurin* is genitive and nunated; this is on the basis of unpacking the compound. The author of *al-Lawami'h* said: and according to this reading, which is the reading of one who reads *a'shurin* as indeclinable or inflected insofar as it is a plural, it follows that the angels who are over the Fire are ninety angels. End. There is some abridgement in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It has also been read *tis'atu a'shurin*, the plural of *'asir*, like *yamin* and *ayman*. End.

This Sulayman ibn Qunna is the one who praised the family of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he is the one who said:

*I passed by the dwellings of the family of Muhammad,*
*and I did not see their like on the day they dismounted.*
*They were a support, then they became a calamity;*
*indeed those calamities have grown great and immense.*

﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire but angels﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], meaning: We made them a creation against which no one among the people has any power. ﴿And We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], meaning: a cause of trial. ﴿A trial﴾ is the second object of *ja'alna* (We made), meaning: We made that number, which is nineteen, a cause of trial for the disbelievers. So ﴿a trial﴾ is not an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). Their trial is that they showed their defiance in their opposition, and that was by way of mockery, for they deny the Resurrection, the Fire and its guardians.

﴿So that they may be certain﴾ (*li-yastayqina*): this is an object of purpose, and it is connected to *ja'alna*, not to *fitna*. So the trial is not caused by certainty; rather the caused element is that making the number a cause for *fitna* [for] ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, and they are the Jews and the Christians, [who are certain] that this Qur'an is from God, since they find this number in their revealed books, and they know that the Messenger did not read it, nor did anyone read it to him, but his Book confirms the books of the prophets, since all of that is truth that supports one another from God Most High. This meaning was stated by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. By the arrival of the realities from God Most High, every person of faith increases in faith, and doubt is removed from those among the People of the Book who affirm, and from the believers.

It is said: the number became a trial only because they mock and say, "Why were they not twenty? And what requires that this number be specified for existence?" They say: this small number, by punishing the majority of the world of jinn and humans from the first of God's creation until the Hour is established, is strong.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: he made the disbelievers' being tested by the number of the guardians a cause for the certainty of the People of the Book and the increase of faith of the believers and the mockery of the disbelievers and the hypocrites, so what is the correct way of understanding that?" I answer: He did not make their being tested by the number the cause of that; rather the number itself is what was made the cause. That is because what is meant by His saying, ﴿And We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31], is: "And We have not made their number but nineteen." So he placed ﴿a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ in the position of *nineteen*, because the state of this number, lacking one from the decade of twenty, is that whoever does not believe in God and His wisdom will be tested by it, and will object, mock, and not submit with the submission of a believer, even if the wisdom behind it is hidden from him. It is as if it were said: "We have made their number a number whose nature is that it tests, in order to make the believers certain and the disbelievers bewildered." End. This is a strange question and an answer in which there is distortion of the Book of God Most High, for he claimed that the meaning of ﴿but as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ is: "but nineteen." No sensible person, nor anyone with the least intelligence, would go to this. Sufficient as a refutation of it is the distortion of the Book of God and the placing of words different from [its] words and a meaning different from [its] meaning.

It is said: *li-yastayqina* is connected to a hidden verb, meaning: "We did that so that they may be certain."

﴿And that they may not doubt﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31]: this is an emphasis on His saying *li-yastayqina*, since affirming certainty and negating doubt is more eloquent and more emphatic in description, for the complete tranquility of the soul.

As for ﴿and those in whose hearts is a sickness﴾: al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: the surah is Meccan, and there was no hypocrisy in Mecca; the sickness in the verse is rather agitation and weakness of faith. It is also said: it is a report of the unseen, meaning: and that the hypocrites, who will plot in the future time in Medina after the Hijra, may say: ﴿What did God intend by this as a parable?﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31]. When they heard this number, they were not guided and were bewildered, so some of them asked others about it, considering it far-fetched that this could be from God; they called it a "parable" (*mathal*) metaphorically, from the parable that is struck, out of astonishment at this number. The meaning is: "What did God intend by this wondrous number?" Their intention was to deny its very origin, and that it is not from God. The grammatical analysis of such a sentence has been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 74, verse 11–30 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾: There is no disagreement that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. It is narrated that he was nicknamed "al-Wahid" (the Unique), meaning because he had no equal in his wealth and in the honour of his household. It has also been said: it is a circumstantial qualifier of the object pronoun in "dharni" (leave me), as Mujahid said, meaning: leave me alone with him, for I will requite you in taking vengeance upon him. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier of the "ta" in "khalaqtu" (I created), meaning: I created him alone, none shared with Me in My creation, so I will destroy him, and I do not need a helper in destroying him. It has also been said: "wahidan" means one whose father is not known. Al-Walid was known to be an illegitimate child (da'iyy), as was mentioned earlier in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Cruel, and after that, of doubtful lineage﴾ [al-Qalam: 13].
