Whoever makes it connected to ﴿قُمْ﴾ at the beginning of the surah, or to ﴿فَأَنْذِرْ﴾ at the beginning of the surah, or a ḥāl from ﴿الْكُبَرِ﴾, or a ḥāl from the pronoun of ﴿الْكُبَرِ﴾ — that is far from the correct. Abu al-Baqa' said: "The preferred view is that it is a ḥāl from what the sentence indicates, its estimate being: 'it has become great as a warning.'" End of quote, and this is a view that is not objectionable.

Al-Naḥḥas said: the hāʾ was dropped from ﴿نَذِيرًا﴾, even though it refers to the Fire, in the sense of the nisba (relative adjective), i.e., possessing the quality of warning. ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: "I mean nadhīran." Al-Hasan said: "[It is] to warn, since it is from the Fire." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this view requires that nadhīran be a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾, or from His saying ﴿لَإِحْدَى﴾. Abu Razin said: nadhīr here is Allah, the Exalted, so it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "call upon the Warner." Ibn Zayd said: nadhīr here is Muhammad ﷺ, so it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "proclaim," or "convey," or "announce." Ubayy and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read ﴿نَذِيرٌ﴾ with a ḍamma. If it describes the Fire, it may be a predicate and the predicate of a suppressed subject, i.e., "it is a warner." If it describes Allah or the Messenger, then it is by a suppressed "he is." The apparent [meaning] is that ﴿لِمَن﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿لِلْبَشَرِ﴾ by repeating the preposition; and ﴿أَن يَتَقَدَّمَ﴾ is a verb in the accusative governed by ﴿شَاءَ﴾, with a pronoun referring to ﴿مَن﴾. It was said: the agent is a pronoun referring to Allah, the Exalted, i.e., "for whoever wills — He (i.e., Allah) — that is, Allah, the Exalted." Al-Hasan said: it is a threat, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is an explanation of the warning and an informing that everyone who follows the path of guidance and truth, if he investigates carefully, will likewise lag behind this rank through his heedlessness and bad reflection. Then he strengthened this meaning with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿أَن يَتَقَدَّمَ﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿لِمَن شَاءَ﴾ is a predicate placed before it, like your saying to one who has performed ablution: "that he pray." Its meaning is absolute: for whoever wills to go forward or to lag behind, that he go forward or lag behind. The intended meaning of going forward and lagging behind is hastening to good and holding back from it. It is like His saying: ﴿فَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. End of quote. This is a meaning that does not come readily to the mind, and in it there is an omission. It was said: going forward is faith and lagging behind is disbelief. Al-Suddi said: "that he go forward toward the Fire previously mentioned, or lag behind from it toward Paradise." Al-Zajjaj said: "that he go forward toward the commanded acts, or lag behind from the forbidden acts." The apparent [meaning] is generality in ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ﴾. Al-Dahhak said: every soul is deserving of punishment, and Allah does not hold any of the people of Paradise in pledge. ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ has the meaning of rahn (pledge), like shatīma with the meaning of shatm (insult), and it is not in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl), because it is without the feminine tāʾ for the masculine and the feminine, as in: rajul qatīl and imraʾa qatīl. So the meaning is: every soul, for what it has earned, is a pledge. From this is the saying of the poet:

Far away is that which is in al-Naʿf, the naʿaf of Kuwaykib,
a pledge of a grave of dust and gravel.

That is: "the grave of a pledge," and the meaning is that every soul is a pledge with Allah, not to be released. It was said: the hāʾ in ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ is for emphasis. It was said: it is according to the feminine form of the word, not with reference to the human being. What I prefer is that it is among those [forms] in which the tāʾ enters, even if it is in the sense of the passive participle originally, like naṭīḥa. What points to this is that when it is a predicate about the masculine it is without hāʾ; He, the Exalted, said: ﴿كُلُّ امْرِئٍ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينٌ﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 21]. So you see that where it is a predicate about the masculine it comes without tāʾ, and where it is a predicate about the feminine it comes with tāʾ, as in this verse. As for the one in the poem, it was made feminine according to the meaning of nafs (soul).

﴿إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the angels. ʿAli said: they are the children of the Muslims. According to these two views it is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), i.e., "but the companions of the right are in gardens." Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: they are the sincere Muslims, who are not held in pledge, because they have paid what was upon them. This is like the saying of al-Dahhak previously mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ﴾ (p-380) — for they have freed their necks from it by what they have made pure of their earnings, as the one who holds a pledge redeems his pledge by paying the right. End of quote. The apparent [meaning] of this is that it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil).

In gardens they will ask one another, about the guilty, [saying]: "What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor, and we used to plunge into vain talk with those who plunged, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment, until certainty came to us." So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them. What is the matter with them, that they turn away from the Reminder, as though they were startled donkeys fleeing from a lion?

Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open. No indeed! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter. No indeed! Indeed, it is a Reminder, so whoever wills may remember it. And they will not remember unless God wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.

[Translator's note omitted per instructions: the passage below is rendered as it stands in the commentary.]

In gardens they [the people of the right] ask one another. Or they ask others about those of their acquaintances who are absent. When they learn that they [the guilty] are in the Fire, they say to them, or the angels say to them, so has some of them estimated. The closer reading is that the sense is: "They ask one another about the guilty, saying to them, after the asking: 'What has brought you into Saqar?'" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how does His saying 'What has brought you into Saqar' correspond to 'They ask one another about the guilty,' since it is a question addressed to the guilty, whereas the question is about them? That correspondence would have held only if it had been said 'They ask one another about the guilty: what brought them into Saqar?' (I say): 'What has brought you' is not an explanation of the asking about them; rather it is a quotation of the speech of those who were asked about them, since those who were asked convey to the askers what passed between them and the guilty, and so they say: 'We said to them, What has brought you into Saqar? They said: We were not among those who prayed.' However, the speech was delivered in the manner of ellipsis and abbreviation, as is the method of the Revelation in the strangeness of its composition." End. In it there is strain. The more apparent view is that the askers are the ones asking one another, and "What has brought you" is by the implicit assumption of "saying," as we have mentioned. Their asking is a question of rebuke and contempt for them; otherwise, the knowledgeable already understand what caused them to enter the Fire. The answer is that they did not possess the qualities of Islam, such as establishing prayer and giving zakat; then they climbed from that to the greatest matter, which is disbelief and denial of the Day of Judgment, like His saying: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11], then He said: ﴿Then he became one of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17].

"Certainty" means: certainty while denying the Day of Judgment, that is, at the time of death. Ibn Atiyya said: "Certainty, in my view, is the truth of what they used to deny, of the return to God Most High and the Hereafter." The commentators said: certainty is death, and that, in my view, is here a later consequence, because death itself is certain to the disbeliever while he is alive. Rather, the certainty they meant in this verse is the thing they used to deny while they were alive in the world, so they became certain of it after death. Certainty is explained as death only in His saying Most High: ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

﴿So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them﴾: the meaning is not that intercession is made for them and the intercession of those who intercede for them does not benefit. Rather, the meaning is the negation of intercession, so benefit is negated; that is, there are no intercessors for them who would benefit them, in the manner of the line of poetry: "On a road whose landmarks are not followed..." meaning it has no landmark by which one could be guided.

Specifying them with the negation of the intercession of intercessors indicates that there may be intercessions and benefit from them, and hadiths have come affirming this.

﴿So what is the matter with them regarding the Reminder﴾, which is the admonitions of the Qur'an that remind of the Hereafter, (turning away), that is, while the state awaited is the one described. Then He likened them to startled donkeys in the intensity of their aversion and flight from faith and the signs of God Most High. The majority read "ḥumur" with a damma on the mim; al-A'mash read it with sukun. Ibn Abbas said: the intended meaning is wild donkeys; He likened them to donkeys as blame and disgrace for them. Nafi', Ibn Amir, and al-Mufaddal from Asim read "mustanfiratun" with a fatha on the fa', and the meaning is: their fright from the qaswara made them flee. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra, that is, fleeing. Nafara and istanfara have the sense of 'ajiba and ista'jaba, and sakhira and istaskhara, and from it is the poet's saying: "Hold your donkey, for it is startled, pursuing she-asses that were accustomed to the Arabs." The kasra is consistent with His saying "farrat" [fled]. Muhammad ibn Sallam said: I asked Abu Sirar al-Ghanawi, who was an eloquent Bedouin, and I said: "As if they were donkeys, what is 'mustanfiratun'?" He said: "A qaswara drove them." I said: "It is only ﴿fled from a lion﴾," He said: "Did they flee?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then it is mustanfiratun."

Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Qatada, and Ikrima said: al-qaswara means the archers. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Hurayra and most of the lexicographers: the lion. Ibn Jubayr said: the men of the hunt, which is close to the first view, and Ibn Abbas also said it. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-qaswara is the beginning of the night, and the meaning is: they fled from the darkness of the night, and nothing is more startled than wild donkeys, and for this reason the Arabs likened camels to them in the speed and lightness of their pace.

﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open﴾, that is, of those who turn away from God's admonitions and signs. ﴿Scrolls spread open﴾ means unfolded, not rolled up, read like the letters exchanged between people, or written in the heavens and brought down by the angels at the moment they were written, fresh and not yet folded. That is because they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "We will not follow you until each one of us is given a book from heaven, its address: from the Lord of the worlds to so-and-so son of so-and-so, in which he is commanded to follow you." Similar is His saying: ﴿We will not believe in your ascending until you bring down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra: 93]. It is narrated that some of them said: "If in scrolls is written what every person does, then let those scrolls be shown to us," and this verse was revealed. The majority read "suhufan" with damma on the sad and ha', and "munashsharatan" with shadda. Ibn Jubayr read it with sukun, "munshharatan," without shadda; nashara and anshara are like nazala and anzala. He likened the unfolding of the scroll to God's resurrecting the dead, so He expressed it as "munashsharatan" from unshirat; what is known for a scroll and a garment is nushira, lightly and triliterally, and it is said of the dead: God resurrected him (anshara-hu), so he was resurrected (nushira), that is, He gave him life so he came to life.

﴿No indeed!﴾ is a rebuke against their desire for that and a restraining of them from demanding signs. ﴿Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter﴾, and for this reason they turned away from the Reminder, not because giving scrolls is impossible. The majority read "yakhafuna" with the third-person ya'; Abu Haywa read it with the second-person ta' as an iltifat (shift). ﴿No indeed!﴾ is a rebuke against their aversion from the Reminder. ﴿Indeed, it is a Reminder﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾: there is a remembrance in its being and in its remembrance, since the Reminder is a remembrance. Nafi', Sallam, and Ya'qub read "tadhkiratun" with the ta' of address and a sukun on the dhal. The rest of the seven, Abu Ja'far, al-A'mash, Talha, Isa, and al-A'raj read it with ya'. It is narrated from Abu Haywa: "yadhdhakkarun" with the third-person ya' and shadda on the dhal. It is narrated from Abu Ja'far: "tadhdhakkarun" with ta' and assimilation of the first ta' into the dhal.

﴿He is the One deserving of piety﴾, that is, deserving to be feared and dreaded, and deserving to forgive. Anas ibn Malik (may God be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained this verse, saying: "Your Lord, whose power and majesty are exalted, says: I am deserving to be feared; so let no other god be feared besides Me, and whoever fears that he should make another god alongside Me, I will forgive him."

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding His saying Most High ﴿And they will not remember unless God wills﴾: that is, unless He compels them to remembrance and forces them to it, since they are sealed upon their hearts, and it is known that they will not believe by choice.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 74, verses 31–56 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him. And it is nothing but a reminder to mankind.﴾ ﴿Nay, by the moon,﴾ ﴿and by the night when it turns back,﴾ ﴿and by the morning when it brightens,﴾ ﴿indeed it is one of the greatest [calamities],﴾ ﴿a warning to mankind,﴾ ﴿to whichever of you wills to go forward or to lag behind.﴾ ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned,﴾ ﴿except the companions of the right,﴾ ﴿in gardens, they will ask one another﴾ ﴿about the criminals,﴾ ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "We were not among those who prayed,﴾ ﴿nor did we feed the poor,﴾ ﴿and we used to plunge in with those who plunged,﴾ ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment,﴾ ﴿until the certainty came to us."﴾ ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them.﴾ ﴿Why are they turning away from the reminder,﴾ ﴿as if they were startled donkeys﴾ ﴿fleeing from a lion?﴾ ﴿Rather, each one of them wishes to be given scrolls spread out.﴾ ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿No! Indeed it is a reminder.﴾ ﴿So whoever wills, let him remember it.﴾ ﴿But they will not remember, unless Allah wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.﴾

The kaf (ﻙ) in ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ is in the accusative position (fi mahall nasb), and ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ refers to what precedes it of the meaning of misguidance and guidance. That is, "like that, [i.e., like] the misguidance and guidance mentioned: He leads astray the disbelievers, so they doubt and He increases them in disbelief and error, and He guides the believers, so He increases them in faith."

﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ is an informing that the matter is beyond what is imagined, and that the recompense is only for a part of His power, not for all of it. The heaven is filled with various kinds of angels. In the hadith: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is not a space of a foot in it but an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah."

﴿وَمَا هِيَ﴾ (and what is it?) means: the Fire, as said by Mujahid; or the address and the warning; or the Fire of this world; or the verses that were mentioned; or the number nineteen; or the hosts. The sayings are several, the most preferred of which is the first, namely Saqar, by which He reminds mankind so that they may fear and obey. The mention of the Fire has also occurred in His saying: ﴿وَمَا جَعَلْنَا أَصْحَابَ النَّارِ إِلَّا مَلَائِكَةً﴾.

﴿إِلَّا ذِكْرَى لِلْبَشَرِ﴾ means: those who are fit for remembrance and taking heed. (Nay) — al-Zamakhshari said: "Nay is a denial after He has made it a reminder: [it cannot be] that they have a reminder, because they do not remember." End of quote. This is not permissible with regard to Allah, the Exalted, that He should inform that it is a reminder for mankind and then deny that it is a reminder for them. Rather, His saying "for mankind" is a general term that is specified. Al-Zamakhshari also said: "Or it is a deterrent to whoever denies that it is one of the greatest [calamities] and a warning." It was also said: it is a deterrent to the saying of Abu Jahl and his companions that they are able to resist the guardians of Hell. It was said: it is a deterrent against mocking the specified number. Al-Farra' said: it is a connective for the oath, and some of them estimated it as ḥaqqan (truly), and some as the initiatory ألا (alā), and the discussion of it has already passed at the end of surah Maryam, peace be upon her.

﴿وَالْقَمَرِ﴾ ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ إِذْ أَدْبَرَ﴾: i.e., it turned back (wallā). It is said that dabara and adbara have one meaning. Allah swore by these things to honor them and to draw attention to what appears through them and within them of the wonders of Allah and His power, and the subsistence of existence depends on their creation.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Yaʿmar, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Abu al-Zinad, Qatada, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, al-Hasan, Talha, the two grammarians, the two sons, and Abu Bakr read: ﴿إِذَا﴾ as a temporal adverb of future time, with dabara with a fatḥa on the dāl. Ibn Jubayr, al-Sulami, and al-Hasan (with a variant transmitted from them) also read it so. Ibn Sirin, al-Aʿraj, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Shaykh, Ibn Muḥaysin, Nafiʿ, Hamza and Ḥafs read: ﴿إِذْ﴾ as a temporal adverb of past time, and ﴿أَدْبَرَ﴾ in the quadriliteral form. Also al-Hasan, Abu Razin, Abu Raja', Ibn Yaʿmar also, al-Sulami also, Talha also, al-Aʿmash, Yunus ibn ʿUbayd and Matar read: ﴿إِذَا﴾ with an alif, ﴿أَدْبَرَ﴾ with a hamza. So it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and Ubayy, and it is suitable with His saying ﴿إِذَا أَسْفَرَ﴾. It is said: "like the past yesterday (kaʾamsi al-dābir)" and "yesterday that has turned back (amsu al-mudbir)" have one meaning.

Yunus ibn Ḥabib said: dabara means "it ended," and adbara means "it turned away." Qatada said: dabara al-layl means "it turned away." Al-Zamakhshari said: dabara has the meaning of adbara, as qabala has the meaning of aqbala. It was also said: it is from dabara al-layl al-nahar, meaning he (the night) succeeded it (the day).

The majority read ﴿أَسْفَرَ﴾ in the quadriliteral form. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ and ʿIsa ibn al-Faḍl read safara in the triliteral form. The meaning: it cast off the darkness from its face.

﴿إِنَّهَا لَإِحْدَى الْكُبَرِ﴾: The apparent [reading] is that the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾ refers to the Fire. It was said: it may be that it refers to the warning, and the matter of the Hereafter; then it is for the circumstance and the story (the pronoun of the situation). It was said: the Hour is "one of the greatest," so the pronoun returns to something not mentioned. The meaning of ﴿إِحْدَى الْكُبَرِ﴾ is "the greatest calamities," i.e., there is no equal to it, as you say: "he is one of the men" (aḥad al-rijāl), and "she is one of the women" (iḥdā al-nisāʾ). Al-Kubar means the greatest of punishments. The reciter said:

O son of al-Muʿalla, the greatest of calamities has descended,
the calamity of time and its deafening changes.

Al-Kubar is the plural of al-kubrā; the feminine alif was dropped in the plural, as its hamza was dropped in qāṣiʿāʾ, so they said qawāṣiʿ. In the book of Ibn ʿAṭiyya: "wa-al-kubar" is the plural of kabīra, and perhaps this is an error of the copyist. The majority read ﴿لَإِحْدَى﴾ with a hamza, and it is changed from a waw, its original being lawiḥdā, and it is an obligatory substitution (badal lāzim). Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Muḥaysin, Wahb ibn Jarīr, from Ibn Kathir, read it with the hamza omitted; this omission is not regular, and the lightening of such a hamza is to make it between-between (bayn bayn). The apparent [meaning] is that this sentence is the answer to the oath. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it is a cause for ﴿كَلَّا﴾ and the oath is an interjection for emphasis." (p-379) End of quote.

The majority read ﴿نَذِيرًا﴾. It is possible that it is a verbal noun with the meaning of "warning," like nakīr with the meaning of inkār (denial), so it is a specification (tamyīz) — i.e., "indeed it is one of the greatest [calamities] as a warning," as you say: "she is one of the women in chastity." Just as iḥdā is given the meaning of "greater," the specification follows it. Al-Farra' said: it is a verbal noun governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "warn with a warning." It is possible that it is an active participle with the meaning of "warner" (mundhir). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾. It was said: it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿إِحْدَى﴾. Whoever makes it connected to ﴿قُمْ﴾ at the beginning of the surah, or to ﴿فَأَنْذِرْ﴾ at the beginning of the surah, or a ḥāl from ﴿الْكُبَرِ﴾, or a ḥāl from the pronoun of ﴿الْكُبَرِ﴾ — that is far from the correct. Abu al-Baqa' said: "The preferred view is that it is a ḥāl from what the sentence indicates, its estimate being: 'it has become great as a warning.'" End of quote, and this is a view that is not objectionable.

Al-Naḥḥas said: the hāʾ was dropped from ﴿نَذِيرًا﴾, even though it refers to the Fire, in the sense of the nisba (relative adjective), i.e., possessing the quality of warning. ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: "I mean nadhīran." Al-Hasan said: "[It is] to warn, since it is from the Fire." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this view requires that nadhīran be a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾, or from His saying ﴿لَإِحْدَى﴾. Abu Razin said: nadhīr here is Allah, the Exalted, so it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "call upon the Warner." Ibn Zayd said: nadhīr here is Muhammad ﷺ, so it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "proclaim," or "convey," or "announce." Ubayy and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read ﴿نَذِيرٌ﴾ with a ḍamma. If it describes the Fire, it may be a predicate and the predicate of a suppressed subject, i.e., "it is a warner." If it describes Allah or the Messenger, then it is by a suppressed "he is." The apparent [meaning] is that ﴿لِمَن﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿لِلْبَشَرِ﴾ by repeating the preposition; and ﴿أَن يَتَقَدَّمَ﴾ is a verb in the accusative governed by ﴿شَاءَ﴾, with a pronoun referring to ﴿مَن﴾. It was said: the agent is a pronoun referring to Allah, the Exalted, i.e., "for whoever wills — He (i.e., Allah) — that is, Allah, the Exalted." Al-Hasan said: it is a threat, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is an explanation of the warning and an informing that everyone who follows the path of guidance and truth, if he investigates carefully, will likewise lag behind this rank through his heedlessness and bad reflection. Then he strengthened this meaning with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿أَن يَتَقَدَّمَ﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿لِمَن شَاءَ﴾ is a predicate placed before it, like your saying to one who has performed ablution: "that he pray." Its meaning is absolute: for whoever wills to go forward or to lag behind, that he go forward or lag behind. The intended meaning of going forward and lagging behind is hastening to good and holding back from it. It is like His saying: ﴿فَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. End of quote. This is a meaning that does not come readily to the mind, and in it there is an omission. It was said: going forward is faith and lagging behind is disbelief. Al-Suddi said: "that he go forward toward the Fire previously mentioned, or lag behind from it toward Paradise." Al-Zajjaj said: "that he go forward toward the commanded acts, or lag behind from the forbidden acts." The apparent [meaning] is generality in ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ﴾. Al-Dahhak said: every soul is deserving of punishment, and Allah does not hold any of the people of Paradise in pledge. ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ has the meaning of rahn (pledge), like shatīma with the meaning of shatm (insult), and it is not in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl), because it is without the feminine tāʾ for the masculine and the feminine, as in: rajul qatīl and imraʾa qatīl. So the meaning is: every soul, for what it has earned, is a pledge. From this is the saying of the poet:

Far away is that which is in al-Naʿf, the naʿaf of Kuwaykib,
a pledge of a grave of dust and gravel.

That is: "the grave of a pledge," and the meaning is that every soul is a pledge with Allah, not to be released. It was said: the hāʾ in ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ is for emphasis. It was said: it is according to the feminine form of the word, not with reference to the human being. What I prefer is that it is among those [forms] in which the tāʾ enters, even if it is in the sense of the passive participle originally, like naṭīḥa. What points to this is that when it is a predicate about the masculine it is without hāʾ; He, the Exalted, said: ﴿كُلُّ امْرِئٍ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينٌ﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 21]. So you see that where it is a predicate about the masculine it comes without tāʾ, and where it is a predicate about the feminine it comes with tāʾ, as in this verse. As for the one in the poem, it was made feminine according to the meaning of nafs (soul).

﴿إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the angels. ʿAli said: they are the children of the Muslims. According to these two views it is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), i.e., "but the companions of the right are in gardens." Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: they are the sincere Muslims, who are not held in pledge, because they have paid what was upon them. This is like the saying of al-Dahhak previously mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ﴾ (p-380) — for they have freed their necks from it by what they have made pure of their earnings, as the one who holds a pledge redeems his pledge by paying the right. End of quote. The apparent [meaning] of this is that it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil).

In gardens they will ask one another, about the guilty, [saying]: "What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor, and we used to plunge into vain talk with those who plunged, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment, until certainty came to us." So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them. What is the matter with them, that they turn away from the Reminder, as though they were startled donkeys fleeing from a lion?

Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open. No indeed! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter. No indeed! Indeed, it is a Reminder, so whoever wills may remember it. And they will not remember unless God wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.

[Translator's note omitted per instructions: the passage below is rendered as it stands in the commentary.]

In gardens they [the people of the right] ask one another. Or they ask others about those of their acquaintances who are absent. When they learn that they [the guilty] are in the Fire, they say to them, or the angels say to them, so has some of them estimated. The closer reading is that the sense is: "They ask one another about the guilty, saying to them, after the asking: 'What has brought you into Saqar?'" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how does His saying 'What has brought you into Saqar' correspond to 'They ask one another about the guilty,' since it is a question addressed to the guilty, whereas the question is about them? That correspondence would have held only if it had been said 'They ask one another about the guilty: what brought them into Saqar?' (I say): 'What has brought you' is not an explanation of the asking about them; rather it is a quotation of the speech of those who were asked about them, since those who were asked convey to the askers what passed between them and the guilty, and so they say: 'We said to them, What has brought you into Saqar? They said: We were not among those who prayed.' However, the speech was delivered in the manner of ellipsis and abbreviation, as is the method of the Revelation in the strangeness of its composition." End. In it there is strain. The more apparent view is that the askers are the ones asking one another, and "What has brought you" is by the implicit assumption of "saying," as we have mentioned. Their asking is a question of rebuke and contempt for them; otherwise, the knowledgeable already understand what caused them to enter the Fire. The answer is that they did not possess the qualities of Islam, such as establishing prayer and giving zakat; then they climbed from that to the greatest matter, which is disbelief and denial of the Day of Judgment, like His saying: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11], then He said: ﴿Then he became one of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17].

"Certainty" means: certainty while denying the Day of Judgment, that is, at the time of death. Ibn Atiyya said: "Certainty, in my view, is the truth of what they used to deny, of the return to God Most High and the Hereafter." The commentators said: certainty is death, and that, in my view, is here a later consequence, because death itself is certain to the disbeliever while he is alive. Rather, the certainty they meant in this verse is the thing they used to deny while they were alive in the world, so they became certain of it after death. Certainty is explained as death only in His saying Most High: ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

﴿So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them﴾: the meaning is not that intercession is made for them and the intercession of those who intercede for them does not benefit. Rather, the meaning is the negation of intercession, so benefit is negated; that is, there are no intercessors for them who would benefit them, in the manner of the line of poetry: "On a road whose landmarks are not followed..." meaning it has no landmark by which one could be guided.

Specifying them with the negation of the intercession of intercessors indicates that there may be intercessions and benefit from them, and hadiths have come affirming this.

﴿So what is the matter with them regarding the Reminder﴾, which is the admonitions of the Qur'an that remind of the Hereafter, (turning away), that is, while the state awaited is the one described. Then He likened them to startled donkeys in the intensity of their aversion and flight from faith and the signs of God Most High. The majority read "ḥumur" with a damma on the mim; al-A'mash read it with sukun. Ibn Abbas said: the intended meaning is wild donkeys; He likened them to donkeys as blame and disgrace for them. Nafi', Ibn Amir, and al-Mufaddal from Asim read "mustanfiratun" with a fatha on the fa', and the meaning is: their fright from the qaswara made them flee. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra, that is, fleeing. Nafara and istanfara have the sense of 'ajiba and ista'jaba, and sakhira and istaskhara, and from it is the poet's saying: "Hold your donkey, for it is startled, pursuing she-asses that were accustomed to the Arabs." The kasra is consistent with His saying "farrat" [fled]. Muhammad ibn Sallam said: I asked Abu Sirar al-Ghanawi, who was an eloquent Bedouin, and I said: "As if they were donkeys, what is 'mustanfiratun'?" He said: "A qaswara drove them." I said: "It is only ﴿fled from a lion﴾," He said: "Did they flee?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then it is mustanfiratun."

Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Qatada, and Ikrima said: al-qaswara means the archers. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Hurayra and most of the lexicographers: the lion. Ibn Jubayr said: the men of the hunt, which is close to the first view, and Ibn Abbas also said it. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-qaswara is the beginning of the night, and the meaning is: they fled from the darkness of the night, and nothing is more startled than wild donkeys, and for this reason the Arabs likened camels to them in the speed and lightness of their pace.

﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open﴾, that is, of those who turn away from God's admonitions and signs. ﴿Scrolls spread open﴾ means unfolded, not rolled up, read like the letters exchanged between people, or written in the heavens and brought down by the angels at the moment they were written, fresh and not yet folded. That is because they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "We will not follow you until each one of us is given a book from heaven, its address: from the Lord of the worlds to so-and-so son of so-and-so, in which he is commanded to follow you." Similar is His saying: ﴿We will not believe in your ascending until you bring down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra: 93]. It is narrated that some of them said: "If in scrolls is written what every person does, then let those scrolls be shown to us," and this verse was revealed. The majority read "suhufan" with damma on the sad and ha', and "munashsharatan" with shadda. Ibn Jubayr read it with sukun, "munshharatan," without shadda; nashara and anshara are like nazala and anzala. He likened the unfolding of the scroll to God's resurrecting the dead, so He expressed it as "munashsharatan" from unshirat; what is known for a scroll and a garment is nushira, lightly and triliterally, and it is said of the dead: God resurrected him (anshara-hu), so he was resurrected (nushira), that is, He gave him life so he came to life.

﴿No indeed!﴾ is a rebuke against their desire for that and a restraining of them from demanding signs. ﴿Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter﴾, and for this reason they turned away from the Reminder, not because giving scrolls is impossible. The majority read "yakhafuna" with the third-person ya'; Abu Haywa read it with the second-person ta' as an iltifat (shift). ﴿No indeed!﴾ is a rebuke against their aversion from the Reminder. ﴿Indeed, it is a Reminder﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾: there is a remembrance in its being and in its remembrance, since the Reminder is a remembrance. Nafi', Sallam, and Ya'qub read "tadhkiratun" with the ta' of address and a sukun on the dhal. The rest of the seven, Abu Ja'far, al-A'mash, Talha, Isa, and al-A'raj read it with ya'. It is narrated from Abu Haywa: "yadhdhakkarun" with the third-person ya' and shadda on the dhal. It is narrated from Abu Ja'far: "tadhdhakkarun" with ta' and assimilation of the first ta' into the dhal.

﴿He is the One deserving of piety﴾, that is, deserving to be feared and dreaded, and deserving to forgive. Anas ibn Malik (may God be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained this verse, saying: "Your Lord, whose power and majesty are exalted, says: I am deserving to be feared; so let no other god be feared besides Me, and whoever fears that he should make another god alongside Me, I will forgive him."

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding His saying Most High ﴿And they will not remember unless God wills﴾: that is, unless He compels them to remembrance and forces them to it, since they are sealed upon their hearts, and it is known that they will not believe by choice.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 74, verses 31–56 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him. And it is nothing but a reminder to mankind.﴾ ﴿Nay, by the moon,﴾ ﴿and by the night when it turns back,﴾ ﴿and by the morning when it brightens,﴾ ﴿indeed it is one of the greatest [calamities],﴾ ﴿a warning to mankind,﴾ ﴿to whichever of you wills to go forward or to lag behind.﴾ ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned,﴾ ﴿except the companions of the right,﴾ ﴿in gardens, they will ask one another﴾ ﴿about the criminals,﴾ ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "We were not among those who prayed,﴾ ﴿nor did we feed the poor,﴾ ﴿and we used to plunge in with those who plunged,﴾ ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment,﴾ ﴿until the certainty came to us."﴾ ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them.﴾ ﴿Why are they turning away from the reminder,﴾ ﴿as if they were startled donkeys﴾ ﴿fleeing from a lion?﴾ ﴿Rather, each one of them wishes to be given scrolls spread out.﴾ ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿No! Indeed it is a reminder.﴾ ﴿So whoever wills, let him remember it.﴾ ﴿But they will not remember, unless Allah wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.﴾

The kaf (ﻙ) in ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ is in the accusative position (fi mahall nasb), and ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ refers to what precedes it of the meaning of misguidance and guidance. That is, "like that, [i.e., like] the misguidance and guidance mentioned: He leads astray the disbelievers, so they doubt and He increases them in disbelief and error, and He guides the believers, so He increases them in faith."

﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ is an informing that the matter is beyond what is imagined, and that the recompense is only for a part of His power, not for all of it. The heaven is filled with various kinds of angels. In the hadith: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is not a space of a foot in it but an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah."

﴿وَمَا هِيَ﴾ (and what is it?) means: the Fire, as said by Mujahid; or the address and the warning; or the Fire of this world; or the verses that were mentioned; or the number nineteen; or the hosts. The sayings are several, the most preferred of which is the first, namely Saqar, by which He reminds mankind so that they may fear and obey. The mention of the Fire has also occurred in His saying: ﴿وَمَا جَعَلْنَا أَصْحَابَ النَّارِ إِلَّا مَلَائِكَةً﴾.

﴿إِلَّا ذِكْرَى لِلْبَشَرِ﴾ means: those who are fit for remembrance and taking heed. (Nay) — al-Zamakhshari said: "Nay is a denial after He has made it a reminder: [it cannot be] that they have a reminder, because they do not remember." End of quote. This is not permissible with regard to Allah, the Exalted, that He should inform that it is a reminder for mankind and then deny that it is a reminder for them. Rather, His saying "for mankind" is a general term that is specified. Al-Zamakhshari also said: "Or it is a deterrent to whoever denies that it is one of the greatest [calamities] and a warning." It was also said: it is a deterrent to the saying of Abu Jahl and his companions that they are able to resist the guardians of Hell. It was said: it is a deterrent against mocking the specified number. Al-Farra' said: it is a connective for the oath, and some of them estimated it as ḥaqqan (truly), and some as the initiatory ألا (alā), and the discussion of it has already passed at the end of surah Maryam, peace be upon her.

﴿وَالْقَمَرِ﴾ ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ إِذْ أَدْبَرَ﴾: i.e., it turned back (wallā). It is said that dabara and adbara have one meaning. Allah swore by these things to honor them and to draw attention to what appears through them and within them of the wonders of Allah and His power, and the subsistence of existence depends on their creation.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Yaʿmar, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Abu al-Zinad, Qatada, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, al-Hasan, Talha, the two grammarians, the two sons, and Abu Bakr read: ﴿إِذَا﴾ as a temporal adverb of future time, with dabara with a fatḥa on the dāl. Ibn Jubayr, al-Sulami, and al-Hasan (with a variant transmitted from them) also read it so. Ibn Sirin, al-Aʿraj, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Shaykh, Ibn Muḥaysin, Nafiʿ, Hamza and Ḥafs read: ﴿إِذْ﴾ as a temporal adverb of past time, and ﴿أَدْبَرَ﴾ in the quadriliteral form. Also al-Hasan, Abu Razin, Abu Raja', Ibn Yaʿmar also, al-Sulami also, Talha also, al-Aʿmash, Yunus ibn ʿUbayd and Matar read: ﴿إِذَا﴾ with an alif, ﴿أَدْبَرَ﴾ with a hamza. So it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and Ubayy, and it is suitable with His saying ﴿إِذَا أَسْفَرَ﴾. It is said: "like the past yesterday (kaʾamsi al-dābir)" and "yesterday that has turned back (amsu al-mudbir)" have one meaning.

Yunus ibn Ḥabib said: dabara means "it ended," and adbara means "it turned away." Qatada said: dabara al-layl means "it turned away." Al-Zamakhshari said: dabara has the meaning of adbara, as qabala has the meaning of aqbala. It was also said: it is from dabara al-layl al-nahar, meaning he (the night) succeeded it (the day).

The majority read ﴿أَسْفَرَ﴾ in the quadriliteral form. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ and ʿIsa ibn al-Faḍl read safara in the triliteral form. The meaning: it cast off the darkness from its face.

﴿إِنَّهَا لَإِحْدَى الْكُبَرِ﴾: The apparent [reading] is that the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾ refers to the Fire. It was said: it may be that it refers to the warning, and the matter of the Hereafter; then it is for the circumstance and the story (the pronoun of the situation). It was said: the Hour is "one of the greatest," so the pronoun returns to something not mentioned. The meaning of ﴿إِحْدَى الْكُبَرِ﴾ is "the greatest calamities," i.e., there is no equal to it, as you say: "he is one of the men" (aḥad al-rijāl), and "she is one of the women" (iḥdā al-nisāʾ). Al-Kubar means the greatest of punishments. The reciter said:

O son of al-Muʿalla, the greatest of calamities has descended,
the calamity of time and its deafening changes.

Al-Kubar is the plural of al-kubrā; the feminine alif was dropped in the plural, as its hamza was dropped in qāṣiʿāʾ, so they said qawāṣiʿ. In the book of Ibn ʿAṭiyya: "wa-al-kubar" is the plural of kabīra, and perhaps this is an error of the copyist. The majority read ﴿لَإِحْدَى﴾ with a hamza, and it is changed from a waw, its original being lawiḥdā, and it is an obligatory substitution (badal lāzim). Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Muḥaysin, Wahb ibn Jarīr, from Ibn Kathir, read it with the hamza omitted; this omission is not regular, and the lightening of such a hamza is to make it between-between (bayn bayn). The apparent [meaning] is that this sentence is the answer to the oath. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it is a cause for ﴿كَلَّا﴾ and the oath is an interjection for emphasis." (p-379) End of quote.

The majority read ﴿نَذِيرًا﴾. It is possible that it is a verbal noun with the meaning of "warning," like nakīr with the meaning of inkār (denial), so it is a specification (tamyīz) — i.e., "indeed it is one of the greatest [calamities] as a warning," as you say: "she is one of the women in chastity." Just as iḥdā is given the meaning of "greater," the specification follows it. Al-Farra' said: it is a verbal noun governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "warn with a warning." It is possible that it is an active participle with the meaning of "warner" (mundhir). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾. It was said: it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿إِحْدَى﴾. Whoever makes it connected to ﴿قُمْ﴾ at the beginning of the surah, or to ﴿فَأَنْذِرْ﴾ at the beginning of the surah, or a ḥāl from ﴿الْكُبَرِ﴾, or a ḥāl from the pronoun of ﴿الْكُبَرِ﴾ — that is far from the correct. Abu al-Baqa' said: "The preferred view is that it is a ḥāl from what the sentence indicates, its estimate being: 'it has become great as a warning.'" End of quote, and this is a view that is not objectionable.

Al-Naḥḥas said: the hāʾ was dropped from ﴿نَذِيرًا﴾, even though it refers to the Fire, in the sense of the nisba (relative adjective), i.e., possessing the quality of warning. ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: "I mean nadhīran." Al-Hasan said: "[It is] to warn, since it is from the Fire." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this view requires that nadhīran be a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾, or from His saying ﴿لَإِحْدَى﴾. Abu Razin said: nadhīr here is Allah, the Exalted, so it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "call upon the Warner." Ibn Zayd said: nadhīr here is Muhammad ﷺ, so it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "proclaim," or "convey," or "announce." Ubayy and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read ﴿نَذِيرٌ﴾ with a ḍamma. If it describes the Fire, it may be a predicate and the predicate of a suppressed subject, i.e., "it is a warner." If it describes Allah or the Messenger, then it is by a suppressed "he is." The apparent [meaning] is that ﴿لِمَن﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿لِلْبَشَرِ﴾ by repeating the preposition; and ﴿أَن يَتَقَدَّمَ﴾ is a verb in the accusative governed by ﴿شَاءَ﴾, with a pronoun referring to ﴿مَن﴾. It was said: the agent is a pronoun referring to Allah, the Exalted, i.e., "for whoever wills — He (i.e., Allah) — that is, Allah, the Exalted." Al-Hasan said: it is a threat, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is an explanation of the warning and an informing that everyone who follows the path of guidance and truth, if he investigates carefully, will likewise lag behind this rank through his heedlessness and bad reflection. Then he strengthened this meaning with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿أَن يَتَقَدَّمَ﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿لِمَن شَاءَ﴾ is a predicate placed before it, like your saying to one who has performed ablution: "that he pray." Its meaning is absolute: for whoever wills to go forward or to lag behind, that he go forward or lag behind. The intended meaning of going forward and lagging behind is hastening to good and holding back from it. It is like His saying: ﴿فَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. End of quote. This is a meaning that does not come readily to the mind, and in it there is an omission. It was said: going forward is faith and lagging behind is disbelief. Al-Suddi said: "that he go forward toward the Fire previously mentioned, or lag behind from it toward Paradise." Al-Zajjaj said: "that he go forward toward the commanded acts, or lag behind from the forbidden acts." The apparent [meaning] is generality in ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ﴾. Al-Dahhak said: every soul is deserving of punishment, and Allah does not hold any of the people of Paradise in pledge. ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ has the meaning of rahn (pledge), like shatīma with the meaning of shatm (insult), and it is not in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl), because it is without the feminine tāʾ for the masculine and the feminine, as in: rajul qatīl and imraʾa qatīl. So the meaning is: every soul, for what it has earned, is a pledge. From this is the saying of the poet:

Far away is that which is in al-Naʿf, the naʿaf of Kuwaykib,
a pledge of a grave of dust and gravel.

That is: "the grave of a pledge," and the meaning is that every soul is a pledge with Allah, not to be released. It was said: the hāʾ in ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ is for emphasis. It was said: it is according to the feminine form of the word, not with reference to the human being. What I prefer is that it is among those [forms] in which the tāʾ enters, even if it is in the sense of the passive participle originally, like naṭīḥa. What points to this is that when it is a predicate about the masculine it is without hāʾ; He, the Exalted, said: ﴿كُلُّ امْرِئٍ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينٌ﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 21]. So you see that where it is a predicate about the masculine it comes without tāʾ, and where it is a predicate about the feminine it comes with tāʾ, as in this verse. As for the one in the poem, it was made feminine according to the meaning of nafs (soul).

﴿إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the angels. ʿAli said: they are the children of the Muslims. According to these two views it is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), i.e., "but the companions of the right are in gardens." Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: they are the sincere Muslims, who are not held in pledge, because they have paid what was upon them. This is like the saying of al-Dahhak previously mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ﴾ (p-380) — for they have freed their necks from it by what they have made pure of their earnings, as the one who holds a pledge redeems his pledge by paying the right. End of quote. The apparent [meaning] of this is that it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil).

In gardens they will ask one another, about the guilty, [saying]: "What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor, and we used to plunge into vain talk with those who plunged, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment, until certainty came to us." So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them. What is the matter with them, that they turn away from the Reminder, as though they were startled donkeys fleeing from a lion?

Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open. No indeed! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter. No indeed! Indeed, it is a Reminder, so whoever wills may remember it. And they will not remember unless God wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.

[Translator's note omitted per instructions: the passage below is rendered as it stands in the commentary.]

In gardens they [the people of the right] ask one another. Or they ask others about those of their acquaintances who are absent. When they learn that they [the guilty] are in the Fire, they say to them, or the angels say to them, so has some of them estimated. The closer reading is that the sense is: "They ask one another about the guilty, saying to them, after the asking: 'What has brought you into Saqar?'" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how does His saying 'What has brought you into Saqar' correspond to 'They ask one another about the guilty,' since it is a question addressed to the guilty, whereas the question is about them? That correspondence would have held only if it had been said 'They ask one another about the guilty: what brought them into Saqar?' (I say): 'What has brought you' is not an explanation of the asking about them; rather it is a quotation of the speech of those who were asked about them, since those who were asked convey to the askers what passed between them and the guilty, and so they say: 'We said to them, What has brought you into Saqar? They said: We were not among those who prayed.' However, the speech was delivered in the manner of ellipsis and abbreviation, as is the method of the Revelation in the strangeness of its composition." End. In it there is strain. The more apparent view is that the askers are the ones asking one another, and "What has brought you" is by the implicit assumption of "saying," as we have mentioned. Their asking is a question of rebuke and contempt for them; otherwise, the knowledgeable already understand what caused them to enter the Fire. The answer is that they did not possess the qualities of Islam, such as establishing prayer and giving zakat; then they climbed from that to the greatest matter, which is disbelief and denial of the Day of Judgment, like His saying: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11], then He said: ﴿Then he became one of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17].

"Certainty" means: certainty while denying the Day of Judgment, that is, at the time of death. Ibn Atiyya said: "Certainty, in my view, is the truth of what they used to deny, of the return to God Most High and the Hereafter." The commentators said: certainty is death, and that, in my view, is here a later consequence, because death itself is certain to the disbeliever while he is alive. Rather, the certainty they meant in this verse is the thing they used to deny while they were alive in the world, so they became certain of it after death. Certainty is explained as death only in His saying Most High: ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

﴿So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them﴾: the meaning is not that intercession is made for them and the intercession of those who intercede for them does not benefit. Rather, the meaning is the negation of intercession, so benefit is negated; that is, there are no intercessors for them who would benefit them, in the manner of the line of poetry: "On a road whose landmarks are not followed..." meaning it has no landmark by which one could be guided.

Specifying them with the negation of the intercession of intercessors indicates that there may be intercessions and benefit from them, and hadiths have come affirming this.

﴿So what is the matter with them regarding the Reminder﴾, which is the admonitions of the Qur'an that remind of the Hereafter, (turning away), that is, while the state awaited is the one described. Then He likened them to startled donkeys in the intensity of their aversion and flight from faith and the signs of God Most High. The majority read "ḥumur" with a damma on the mim; al-A'mash read it with sukun. Ibn Abbas said: the intended meaning is wild donkeys; He likened them to donkeys as blame and disgrace for them. Nafi', Ibn Amir, and al-Mufaddal from Asim read "mustanfiratun" with a fatha on the fa', and the meaning is: their fright from the qaswara made them flee. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra, that is, fleeing. Nafara and istanfara have the sense of 'ajiba and ista'jaba, and sakhira and istaskhara, and from it is the poet's saying: "Hold your donkey, for it is startled, pursuing she-asses that were accustomed to the Arabs." The kasra is consistent with His saying "farrat" [fled]. Muhammad ibn Sallam said: I asked Abu Sirar al-Ghanawi, who was an eloquent Bedouin, and I said: "As if they were donkeys, what is 'mustanfiratun'?" He said: "A qaswara drove them." I said: "It is only ﴿fled from a lion﴾," He said: "Did they flee?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then it is mustanfiratun."

Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Qatada, and Ikrima said: al-qaswara means the archers. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Hurayra and most of the lexicographers: the lion. Ibn Jubayr said: the men of the hunt, which is close to the first view, and Ibn Abbas also said it. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-qaswara is the beginning of the night, and the meaning is: they fled from the darkness of the night, and nothing is more startled than wild donkeys, and for this reason the Arabs likened camels to them in the speed and lightness of their pace.

﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open﴾, that is, of those who turn away from God's admonitions and signs. ﴿Scrolls spread open﴾ means unfolded, not rolled up, read like the letters exchanged between people, or written in the heavens and brought down by the angels at the moment they were written, fresh and not yet folded. That is because they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "We will not follow you until each one of us is given a book from heaven, its address: from the Lord of the worlds to so-and-so son of so-and-so, in which he is commanded to follow you." Similar is His saying: ﴿We will not believe in your ascending until you bring down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra: 93]. It is narrated that some of them said: "If in scrolls is written what every person does, then let those scrolls be shown to us," and this verse was revealed. The majority read "suhufan" with damma on the sad and ha', and "munashsharatan" with shadda. Ibn Jubayr read it with sukun, "munshharatan," without shadda; nashara and anshara are like nazala and anzala. He likened the unfolding of the scroll to God's resurrecting the dead, so He expressed it as "munashsharatan" from unshirat; what is known for a scroll and a garment is nushira, lightly and triliterally, and it is said of the dead: God resurrected him (anshara-hu), so he was resurrected (nushira), that is, He gave him life so he came to life.

﴿No indeed!﴾ is a rebuke against their desire for that and a restraining of them from demanding signs. ﴿Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter﴾, and for this reason they turned away from the Reminder, not because giving scrolls is impossible. The majority read "yakhafuna" with the third-person ya'; Abu Haywa read it with the second-person ta' as an iltifat (shift). ﴿No indeed!﴾ is a rebuke against their aversion from the Reminder. ﴿Indeed, it is a Reminder﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾: there is a remembrance in its being and in its remembrance, since the Reminder is a remembrance. Nafi', Sallam, and Ya'qub read "tadhkiratun" with the ta' of address and a sukun on the dhal. The rest of the seven, Abu Ja'far, al-A'mash, Talha, Isa, and al-A'raj read it with ya'. It is narrated from Abu Haywa: "yadhdhakkarun" with the third-person ya' and shadda on the dhal. It is narrated from Abu Ja'far: "tadhdhakkarun" with ta' and assimilation of the first ta' into the dhal.

﴿He is the One deserving of piety﴾, that is, deserving to be feared and dreaded, and deserving to forgive. Anas ibn Malik (may God be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained this verse, saying: "Your Lord, whose power and majesty are exalted, says: I am deserving to be feared; so let no other god be feared besides Me, and whoever fears that he should make another god alongside Me, I will forgive him."

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding His saying Most High ﴿And they will not remember unless God wills﴾: that is, unless He compels them to remembrance and forces them to it, since they are sealed upon their hearts, and it is known that they will not believe by choice.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 74, verses 31–56 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him. And it is nothing but a reminder to mankind.﴾ ﴿Nay, by the moon,﴾ ﴿and by the night when it turns back,﴾ ﴿and by the morning when it brightens,﴾ ﴿indeed it is one of the greatest [calamities],﴾ ﴿a warning to mankind,﴾ ﴿to whichever of you wills to go forward or to lag behind.﴾ ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned,﴾ ﴿except the companions of the right,﴾ ﴿in gardens, they will ask one another﴾ ﴿about the criminals,﴾ ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "We were not among those who prayed,﴾ ﴿nor did we feed the poor,﴾ ﴿and we used to plunge in with those who plunged,﴾ ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment,﴾ ﴿until the certainty came to us."﴾ ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them.﴾ ﴿Why are they turning away from the reminder,﴾ ﴿as if they were startled donkeys﴾ ﴿fleeing from a lion?﴾ ﴿Rather, each one of them wishes to be given scrolls spread out.﴾ ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿No! Indeed it is a reminder.﴾ ﴿So whoever wills, let him remember it.﴾ ﴿But they will not remember, unless Allah wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.﴾

The kaf (ﻙ) in ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ is in the accusative position (fi mahall nasb), and ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ refers to what precedes it of the meaning of misguidance and guidance. That is, "like that, [i.e., like] the misguidance and guidance mentioned: He leads astray the disbelievers, so they doubt and He increases them in disbelief and error, and He guides the believers, so He increases them in faith."

﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾ is an informing that the matter is beyond what is imagined, and that the recompense is only for a part of His power, not for all of it. The heaven is filled with various kinds of angels. In the hadith: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is not a space of a foot in it but an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah."

﴿وَمَا هِيَ﴾ (and what is it?) means: the Fire, as said by Mujahid; or the address and the warning; or the Fire of this world; or the verses that were mentioned; or the number nineteen; or the hosts. The sayings are several, the most preferred of which is the first, namely Saqar, by which He reminds mankind so that they may fear and obey. The mention of the Fire has also occurred in His saying: ﴿وَمَا جَعَلْنَا أَصْحَابَ النَّارِ إِلَّا مَلَائِكَةً﴾.

﴿إِلَّا ذِكْرَى لِلْبَشَرِ﴾ means: those who are fit for remembrance and taking heed. (Nay) — al-Zamakhshari said: "Nay is a denial after He has made it a reminder: [it cannot be] that they have a reminder, because they do not remember." End of quote. This is not permissible with regard to Allah, the Exalted, that He should inform that it is a reminder for mankind and then deny that it is a reminder for them. Rather, His saying "for mankind" is a general term that is specified. Al-Zamakhshari also said: "Or it is a deterrent to whoever denies that it is one of the greatest [calamities] and a warning." It was also said: it is a deterrent to the saying of Abu Jahl and his companions that they are able to resist the guardians of Hell. It was said: it is a deterrent against mocking the specified number. Al-Farra' said: it is a connective for the oath, and some of them estimated it as ḥaqqan (truly), and some as the initiatory ألا (alā), and the discussion of it has already passed at the end of surah Maryam, peace be upon her.

﴿وَالْقَمَرِ﴾ ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ إِذْ أَدْبَرَ﴾: i.e., it turned back (wallā). It is said that dabara and adbara have one meaning. Allah swore by these things to honor them and to draw attention to what appears through them and within them of the wonders of Allah and His power, and the subsistence of existence depends on their creation.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Yaʿmar, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Abu al-Zinad, Qatada, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, al-Hasan, Talha, the two grammarians, the two sons, and Abu Bakr read: ﴿إِذَا﴾ as a temporal adverb of future time, with dabara with a fatḥa on the dāl. Ibn Jubayr, al-Sulami, and al-Hasan (with a variant transmitted from them) also read it so. Ibn Sirin, al-Aʿraj, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Abu Shaykh, Ibn Muḥaysin, Nafiʿ, Hamza and Ḥafs read: ﴿إِذْ﴾ as a temporal adverb of past time, and ﴿أَدْبَرَ﴾ in the quadriliteral form. Also al-Hasan, Abu Razin, Abu Raja', Ibn Yaʿmar also, al-Sulami also, Talha also, al-Aʿmash, Yunus ibn ʿUbayd and Matar read: ﴿إِذَا﴾ with an alif, ﴿أَدْبَرَ﴾ with a hamza. So it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and Ubayy, and it is suitable with His saying ﴿إِذَا أَسْفَرَ﴾. It is said: "like the past yesterday (kaʾamsi al-dābir)" and "yesterday that has turned back (amsu al-mudbir)" have one meaning.

Yunus ibn Ḥabib said: dabara means "it ended," and adbara means "it turned away." Qatada said: dabara al-layl means "it turned away." Al-Zamakhshari said: dabara has the meaning of adbara, as qabala has the meaning of aqbala. It was also said: it is from dabara al-layl al-nahar, meaning he (the night) succeeded it (the day).

The majority read ﴿أَسْفَرَ﴾ in the quadriliteral form. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ and ʿIsa ibn al-Faḍl read safara in the triliteral form. The meaning: it cast off the darkness from its face.

﴿إِنَّهَا لَإِحْدَى الْكُبَرِ﴾: The apparent [reading] is that the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾ refers to the Fire. It was said: it may be that it refers to the warning, and the matter of the Hereafter; then it is for the circumstance and the story (the pronoun of the situation). It was said: the Hour is "one of the greatest," so the pronoun returns to something not mentioned. The meaning of ﴿إِحْدَى الْكُبَرِ﴾ is "the greatest calamities," i.e., there is no equal to it, as you say: "he is one of the men" (aḥad al-rijāl), and "she is one of the women" (iḥdā al-nisāʾ). Al-Kubar means the greatest of punishments. The reciter said:

O son of al-Muʿalla, the greatest of calamities has descended,
the calamity of time and its deafening changes.

Al-Kubar is the plural of al-kubrā; the feminine alif was dropped in the plural, as its hamza was dropped in qāṣiʿāʾ, so they said qawāṣiʿ. In the book of Ibn ʿAṭiyya: "wa-al-kubar" is the plural of kabīra, and perhaps this is an error of the copyist. The majority read ﴿لَإِحْدَى﴾ with a hamza, and it is changed from a waw, its original being lawiḥdā, and it is an obligatory substitution (badal lāzim). Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Muḥaysin, Wahb ibn Jarīr, from Ibn Kathir, read it with the hamza omitted; this omission is not regular, and the lightening of such a hamza is to make it between-between (bayn bayn). The apparent [meaning] is that this sentence is the answer to the oath. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it is a cause for ﴿كَلَّا﴾ and the oath is an interjection for emphasis." (p-379) End of quote.

The majority read ﴿نَذِيرًا﴾. It is possible that it is a verbal noun with the meaning of "warning," like nakīr with the meaning of inkār (denial), so it is a specification (tamyīz) — i.e., "indeed it is one of the greatest [calamities] as a warning," as you say: "she is one of the women in chastity." Just as iḥdā is given the meaning of "greater," the specification follows it. Al-Farra' said: it is a verbal noun governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "warn with a warning." It is possible that it is an active participle with the meaning of "warner" (mundhir). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾. It was said: it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿إِحْدَى﴾. Whoever makes it connected to ﴿قُمْ﴾ at the beginning of the surah, or to ﴿فَأَنْذِرْ﴾ at the beginning of the surah, or a ḥāl from ﴿الْكُبَرِ﴾, or a ḥāl from the pronoun of ﴿الْكُبَرِ﴾ — that is far from the correct. Abu al-Baqa' said: "The preferred view is that it is a ḥāl from what the sentence indicates, its estimate being: 'it has become great as a warning.'" End of quote, and this is a view that is not objectionable.

Al-Naḥḥas said: the hāʾ was dropped from ﴿نَذِيرًا﴾, even though it refers to the Fire, in the sense of the nisba (relative adjective), i.e., possessing the quality of warning. ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: "I mean nadhīran." Al-Hasan said: "[It is] to warn, since it is from the Fire." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this view requires that nadhīran be a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿إِنَّهَا﴾, or from His saying ﴿لَإِحْدَى﴾. Abu Razin said: nadhīr here is Allah, the Exalted, so it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "call upon the Warner." Ibn Zayd said: nadhīr here is Muhammad ﷺ, so it is governed by a suppressed verb, i.e., "proclaim," or "convey," or "announce." Ubayy and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read ﴿نَذِيرٌ﴾ with a ḍamma. If it describes the Fire, it may be a predicate and the predicate of a suppressed subject, i.e., "it is a warner." If it describes Allah or the Messenger, then it is by a suppressed "he is." The apparent [meaning] is that ﴿لِمَن﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿لِلْبَشَرِ﴾ by repeating the preposition; and ﴿أَن يَتَقَدَّمَ﴾ is a verb in the accusative governed by ﴿شَاءَ﴾, with a pronoun referring to ﴿مَن﴾. It was said: the agent is a pronoun referring to Allah, the Exalted, i.e., "for whoever wills — He (i.e., Allah) — that is, Allah, the Exalted." Al-Hasan said: it is a threat, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is an explanation of the warning and an informing that everyone who follows the path of guidance and truth, if he investigates carefully, will likewise lag behind this rank through his heedlessness and bad reflection. Then he strengthened this meaning with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿أَن يَتَقَدَّمَ﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿لِمَن شَاءَ﴾ is a predicate placed before it, like your saying to one who has performed ablution: "that he pray." Its meaning is absolute: for whoever wills to go forward or to lag behind, that he go forward or lag behind. The intended meaning of going forward and lagging behind is hastening to good and holding back from it. It is like His saying: ﴿فَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. End of quote. This is a meaning that does not come readily to the mind, and in it there is an omission. It was said: going forward is faith and lagging behind is disbelief. Al-Suddi said: "that he go forward toward the Fire previously mentioned, or lag behind from it toward Paradise." Al-Zajjaj said: "that he go forward toward the commanded acts, or lag behind from the forbidden acts." The apparent [meaning] is generality in ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ﴾. Al-Dahhak said: every soul is deserving of punishment, and Allah does not hold any of the people of Paradise in pledge. ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ has the meaning of rahn (pledge), like shatīma with the meaning of shatm (insult), and it is not in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl), because it is without the feminine tāʾ for the masculine and the feminine, as in: rajul qatīl and imraʾa qatīl. So the meaning is: every soul, for what it has earned, is a pledge. From this is the saying of the poet:

Far away is that which is in al-Naʿf, the naʿaf of Kuwaykib,
a pledge of a grave of dust and gravel.

That is: "the grave of a pledge," and the meaning is that every soul is a pledge with Allah, not to be released. It was said: the hāʾ in ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ is for emphasis. It was said: it is according to the feminine form of the word, not with reference to the human being. What I prefer is that it is among those [forms] in which the tāʾ enters, even if it is in the sense of the passive participle originally, like naṭīḥa. What points to this is that when it is a predicate about the masculine it is without hāʾ; He, the Exalted, said: ﴿كُلُّ امْرِئٍ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينٌ﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 21]. So you see that where it is a predicate about the masculine it comes without tāʾ, and where it is a predicate about the feminine it comes with tāʾ, as in this verse. As for the one in the poem, it was made feminine according to the meaning of nafs (soul).

﴿إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the angels. ʿAli said: they are the children of the Muslims. According to these two views it is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), i.e., "but the companions of the right are in gardens." Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: they are the sincere Muslims, who are not held in pledge, because they have paid what was upon them. This is like the saying of al-Dahhak previously mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ﴾ (p-380) — for they have freed their necks from it by what they have made pure of their earnings, as the one who holds a pledge redeems his pledge by paying the right. End of quote. The apparent [meaning] of this is that it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil).

In gardens they will ask one another, about the guilty, [saying]: "What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor, and we used to plunge into vain talk with those who plunged, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment, until certainty came to us." So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them. What is the matter with them, that they turn away from the Reminder, as though they were startled donkeys fleeing from a lion?

Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open. No indeed! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter. No indeed! Indeed, it is a Reminder, so whoever wills may remember it. And they will not remember unless God wills. He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness.

[Translator's note omitted per instructions: the passage below is rendered as it stands in the commentary.]

In gardens they [the people of the right] ask one another. Or they ask others about those of their acquaintances who are absent. When they learn that they [the guilty] are in the Fire, they say to them, or the angels say to them, so has some of them estimated. The closer reading is that the sense is: "They ask one another about the guilty, saying to them, after the asking: 'What has brought you into Saqar?'" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how does His saying 'What has brought you into Saqar' correspond to 'They ask one another about the guilty,' since it is a question addressed to the guilty, whereas the question is about them? That correspondence would have held only if it had been said 'They ask one another about the guilty: what brought them into Saqar?' (I say): 'What has brought you' is not an explanation of the asking about them; rather it is a quotation of the speech of those who were asked about them, since those who were asked convey to the askers what passed between them and the guilty, and so they say: 'We said to them, What has brought you into Saqar? They said: We were not among those who prayed.' However, the speech was delivered in the manner of ellipsis and abbreviation, as is the method of the Revelation in the strangeness of its composition." End. In it there is strain. The more apparent view is that the askers are the ones asking one another, and "What has brought you" is by the implicit assumption of "saying," as we have mentioned. Their asking is a question of rebuke and contempt for them; otherwise, the knowledgeable already understand what caused them to enter the Fire. The answer is that they did not possess the qualities of Islam, such as establishing prayer and giving zakat; then they climbed from that to the greatest matter, which is disbelief and denial of the Day of Judgment, like His saying: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11], then He said: ﴿Then he became one of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17].

"Certainty" means: certainty while denying the Day of Judgment, that is, at the time of death. Ibn Atiyya said: "Certainty, in my view, is the truth of what they used to deny, of the return to God Most High and the Hereafter." The commentators said: certainty is death, and that, in my view, is here a later consequence, because death itself is certain to the disbeliever while he is alive. Rather, the certainty they meant in this verse is the thing they used to deny while they were alive in the world, so they became certain of it after death. Certainty is explained as death only in His saying Most High: ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

﴿So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them﴾: the meaning is not that intercession is made for them and the intercession of those who intercede for them does not benefit. Rather, the meaning is the negation of intercession, so benefit is negated; that is, there are no intercessors for them who would benefit them, in the manner of the line of poetry: "On a road whose landmarks are not followed..." meaning it has no landmark by which one could be guided.

Specifying them with the negation of the intercession of intercessors indicates that there may be intercessions and benefit from them, and hadiths have come affirming this.

﴿So what is the matter with them regarding the Reminder﴾, which is the admonitions of the Qur'an that remind of the Hereafter, (turning away), that is, while the state awaited is the one described. Then He likened them to startled donkeys in the intensity of their aversion and flight from faith and the signs of God Most High. The majority read "ḥumur" with a damma on the mim; al-A'mash read it with sukun. Ibn Abbas said: the intended meaning is wild donkeys; He likened them to donkeys as blame and disgrace for them. Nafi', Ibn Amir, and al-Mufaddal from Asim read "mustanfiratun" with a fatha on the fa', and the meaning is: their fright from the qaswara made them flee. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra, that is, fleeing. Nafara and istanfara have the sense of 'ajiba and ista'jaba, and sakhira and istaskhara, and from it is the poet's saying: "Hold your donkey, for it is startled, pursuing she-asses that were accustomed to the Arabs." The kasra is consistent with His saying "farrat" [fled]. Muhammad ibn Sallam said: I asked Abu Sirar al-Ghanawi, who was an eloquent Bedouin, and I said: "As if they were donkeys, what is 'mustanfiratun'?" He said: "A qaswara drove them." I said: "It is only ﴿fled from a lion﴾," He said: "Did they flee?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then it is mustanfiratun."

Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Qatada, and Ikrima said: al-qaswara means the archers. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Hurayra and most of the lexicographers: the lion. Ibn Jubayr said: the men of the hunt, which is close to the first view, and Ibn Abbas also said it. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-qaswara is the beginning of the night, and the meaning is: they fled from the darkness of the night, and nothing is more startled than wild donkeys, and for this reason the Arabs likened camels to them in the speed and lightness of their pace.

﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread open﴾, that is, of those who turn away from God's admonitions and signs. ﴿Scrolls spread open﴾ means unfolded, not rolled up, read like the letters exchanged between people, or written in the heavens and brought down by the angels at the moment they were written, fresh and not yet folded. That is because they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "We will not follow you until each one of us is given a book from heaven, its address: from the Lord of the worlds to so-and-so son of so-and-so, in which he is commanded to follow you." Similar is His saying: ﴿We will not believe in your ascending until you bring down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra: 93]. It is narrated that some of them said: "If in scrolls is written what every person does, then let those scrolls be shown to us," and this verse was revealed. The majority read "suhufan" with damma on the sad and ha', and "munashsharatan" with shadda. Ibn Jubayr read it with sukun, "munshharatan," without shadda; nashara and anshara are like nazala and anzala. He likened the unfolding of the scroll to God's resurrecting the dead, so He expressed it as "munashsharatan" from unshirat; what is known for a scroll and a garment is nushira, lightly and triliterally, and it is said of the dead: God resurrected him (anshara-hu), so he was resurrected (nushira), that is, He gave him life so he came to life.

﴿No indeed!﴾ is a rebuke against their desire for that and a restraining of them from demanding signs. ﴿Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter﴾, and for this reason they turned away from the Reminder, not because giving scrolls is impossible. The majority read "yakhafuna" with the third-person ya'; Abu Haywa read it with the second-person ta' as an iltifat (shift). ﴿No indeed!﴾ is a rebuke against their aversion from the Reminder. ﴿Indeed, it is a Reminder﴾ ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾: there is a remembrance in its being and in its remembrance, since the Reminder is a remembrance.
